cc.name: Athens

sights.name: Zenetos's Circular School
sights.blurb: A disc-shaped school of the 1970s wrapped in sun-tuned louvres: the best-known built work of Greece's great utopian modernist.
sights.when: Working state school with about 1,500 pupils: view from outside, not at school-run times.

sights.name: NTUA student residence, Zografou
sights.blurb: A ten-storey béton-brut slab on tall pilotis at the foot of Hymettus, called the building that carries Greek brutalism almost single-handed.
sights.when: In use by students, poor condition; exterior from the street.

sights.name: Lycabettus Theatre
sights.blurb: Zenetos's open-air amphitheatre in an old quarry on the hill, ruined in 2008 and reopened in 2023 with his light roof restored.
sights.when: Events only, roughly mid-May to October; buy a concert ticket to see it.

sights.name: FIX brewery / EMST
sights.blurb: Zenetos's 1957 glass-and-brick skin round an 1864 brewery, half cut away for the metro and now the National Museum of Contemporary Art.

sights.name: Zenetos's block, Amalias 34
sights.blurb: A 1959–60 apartment block with sliding façade panels: the original of the cheap folding shutters later copied all over Athens.

sights.name: Pikionis's Pefkakia school
sights.blurb: Dimitris Pikionis's only fully modernist building, a 1931–32 school stepped down a steep slope; he disowned it almost at once.
sights.when: Working school; view from the street. The map pin is the 14th Primary School, Sina 70; check on site that it is the Pikionis building.

sights.name: Antonakakis block, Em. Benaki 118
sights.blurb: A 1974–75 Exarchia block by Atelier 66 whose stair is an open 'street' climbing through the building.

sights.name: Valsamakis's first block, Semitelou 5
sights.blurb: Nikos Valsamakis's first building, a refined 1950s block near Plateia Mavili.

sights.name: Valsamakis block, Irodotou 17
sights.blurb: A mid-1950s Kolonaki block by Nikos Valsamakis.

sights.name: Valsamakis block, Vas. Konstantinou 42
sights.blurb: A 1959–60 Valsamakis block on Plateia Proskopon, next door to a Molfesis block of the same year.

sights.name: Molfesis block, Vas. Konstantinou 46
sights.blurb: Sthenis Molfesis's 1959 block, by the architect of the unbuilt-or-unknown modern church in Ano Glyfada.

sights.name: Papazisis block, Mithimnis 34
sights.blurb: A 1957–58 block by Dimitris Papazisis off Plateia Amerikis.

sights.name: Antonakakis & Gartzos block, Argolidos 26
sights.blurb: An early (1961–62) block by Suzana and Dimitris Antonakakis with Kostis Gartzos.

sights.name: Kypselis 28
sights.blurb: A 1955 Kypseli block with Corbusian ribbon balconies and bands of Cretan tile.

sights.name: Zolotas house, Dionysiou Areopagitou 27
sights.blurb: Emmanouil Vourekas's austere 1960 house facing the Acropolis, home of the economist and prime minister Xenophon Zolotas.
sights.when: Private; seen from the pedestrian street.

sights.name: Athens Hilton
sights.blurb: The 1959–63 slab that Athenians loved and hated: Vasileiadis, Vourekas and Staikos's 'skyscraper', with incised murals by Yannis Moralis.
sights.when: Hotel; lobby and rooftop bar open to guests and visitors.

sights.name: Athens Tower
sights.blurb: Greece's first glass-curtain skyscraper (1971–73), built in a gap in the height law under the junta.

sights.name: Apollo Tower
sights.blurb: Greece's tallest residential building (1973, 80 m), which stayed lit through the 1981 and 1999 earthquakes on its own generators.

sights.name: ERT Radiomegaro
sights.blurb: The junta-era brutalist broadcasting house, occupied by its workers when the government shut ERT in 2013.

sights.name: Konstantinidis's OEK estate, Nea Filadelfeia
sights.blurb: Aris Konstantinidis's 1955–57 workers' housing: low blocks with a bare concrete frame and earth-coloured infill.
sights.when: Lived-in, altered by residents; street view. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Mont Parnes hotel-casino
sights.blurb: Pavlos Mylonas's 1958–61 hotel at 1,078 m on Parnitha, a casino since 1971, reached by the 1972 cable car.

sights.name: Prosfygika, Alexandras Avenue
sights.blurb: Eight 1930s refugee blocks in reinforced concrete facing the Areos stadium: Athens's own small Falowiec, decayed and still lived in.
sights.when: Lived-in and partly occupied; walk through respectfully. Restoration of 4 of the 8 blocks planned to 2028: expect scaffolding. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Blue Building, Exarchia
sights.blurb: The 1932–33 block on Exarchia Square that Le Corbusier is said to have praised: 'C'est très beau'.

sights.name: Lanara block, Fokionos Negri 23
sights.blurb: The finest interwar block on Kypseli's long pedestrian street (1938), threatened with demolition and listed in 2006.

sights.name: Protopapa block and the first Fokionos Negri blocks
sights.blurb: Fokionos Negri 7 (1932) and 9 (1933): the first modern apartment blocks on the street.

sights.name: Bonis block and 1938 shelter, Kypseli
sights.blurb: A 1938 block whose basement air-raid shelter still has its hand-operated steel doors and lighting.

sights.name: Dourgouti refugee blocks, Neos Kosmos
sights.blurb: Interwar refugee blocks and 1924 row houses in Neos Kosmos, where the Armenian quarter burned in the 1944 blockade.
sights.when: Lived-in; street view. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Tavros refugee estate
sights.blurb: 'Metaxas two-storeys' of 1936 and 71 blocks with over 2,000 flats off Pireos Street.
sights.when: Lived-in; street view. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Olympic Village, Thrakomakedones
sights.blurb: The 2004 athletes' village: the flats are lived in, the admin and sports buildings left to rot; an empty entrance building burned in July 2026.
sights.when: Walk round; derelict buildings fenced and off-limits.

sights.name: Hellinikon: Saarinen terminal and the new park
sights.blurb: The old airport turned building site and park: Eero Saarinen's 1969 terminal, the control tower and hangars kept as relics of a vanished airfield.
sights.when: Sports Park open in stages from 20 July 2026; Experience Centre daily 9–21. The Saarinen terminal is closed. Pin = Experience Centre.

sights.name: Faliro Olympic beach-volleyball stadium
sights.blurb: A 9,600-seat concrete stadium built for beach volleyball in 2004, never used for official competition since: the emblem of Athens's white elephants.
sights.when: Fenced and derelict; view from outside. The Aenaon Park plan will turn it into an open-air events amphitheatre, so see it soon. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Goudi 'Badminton' theatre
sights.blurb: The 2004 badminton hall in Goudi park, converted to a theatre; a fire hit the old building on 12 July 2026.
sights.when: Status after the fire unknown; check before going. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Papadimitriou sanatorium, Penteli
sights.blurb: A 1930s TB sanatorium in the pines of Penteli, used by IKA until 2016, now a looted concrete shell: the heart of Athens's 'Greek Davos'.
sights.when: Fenced; enter at your own risk is not advised. Exterior from the grounds' edge. Plans for an 'Athens Health Park' are in flux.
sights.q: Sismanogleio Annex (former Papadimitriou), Al. Zaimi 5, Melissia

sights.name: Daou sanatorium ruin, Penteli
sights.blurb: A stone prewar sanatorium in 460 stremmata of pine whose staff were in ELAS; a nurse was executed in 1944.

sights.name: Xenia Parnitha
sights.blurb: A 1930s sanatorium turned EOT Xenia hotel turned tourism school, closed in 1980 and stripped to its walls: the most visited ruin in Greece.
sights.when: Open ruin, structurally unsafe after the 1999 quake. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Peloponnese (SPAP) station
sights.blurb: The ornate 19th-century terminus of the metre-gauge line to the Peloponnese, closed in 2005.
sights.when: Closed; restoration status unknown. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Lipasmata Drapetsona (Workers' Park)
sights.blurb: A 2.5 km seafront walk through the remains of one of Europe's largest fertiliser works: chimney, silos, water tower and a conveyor gantry.

sights.name: Peiraiki-Patraiki mill, Megalo Pefko
sights.blurb: The first new factory of postwar Greece (1950), praised by Time in 1962, closed in 1992 and abandoned.

sights.name: Tatoi estate and royal cemetery
sights.blurb: The 42 km² summer estate of Greece's kings, abandoned after 1974, burned in 2021, now being restored: palace, farm, forest and the royal cemetery.
sights.when: Museum core due to open December 2026; until then the grounds and access change. Check before going.

sights.name: Makronisos prison island
sights.blurb: The Civil War 're-education' island off Lavrio: ruined camps and churches on a bare 13 km ridge. Charter boat only.
sights.when: No ferry: charter from Lavrio (Port Authority +30 22920 25249); landing and interpretation minimal; confirm access with the operator.

sights.name: Sotiria hospital 1936 buildings
sights.blurb: The TB hospital where Periklis Georgakopoulos and Ioannis Despotopoulos built some of the key interwar modernist hospital blocks (1936).
sights.when: Working hospital; which blocks survive unaltered is unchecked. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Agios Georgios power station ('Drakos')
sights.blurb: Interwar power station on the Keratsini shore (1928–2012), its red-and-white chimney listed in 2023; scene of the 1944 'Battle of the Electric'.
sights.when: Visits with the history exhibition (since 2017) on set days; exterior from the coast road. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Old Faliro power station (1903)
sights.blurb: Greece's first thermal power station (1903), listed in 1986, its main hall decaying beside the Karaiskakis stadium.
sights.when: Exterior; rare guided visits (Friends of the Benaki) and art events. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: CHROPEI paint works
sights.blurb: A listed paint factory (1899–1989) of nearly 18,000 m², empty on Pireos Street with its neighbours.

sights.name: Pireos 260
sights.blurb: Ten listed concrete factory buildings used for the Athens Festival and earmarked for a Culture Ministry conversion.

sights.name: Marathon dam
sights.blurb: The 1929 dam built by the American firm Ulen, faced entirely in marble, with a small water museum.
sights.when: Crest walkable; EYDAP museum. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Lavrio railway relics, Thorikos
sights.blurb: Traces of the metre-gauge Lavrio line (closed 1957–62): a bridge, rails and a decaying station at Thorikos.

sights.name: Lavrio mining landscape
sights.blurb: Silver mines of classical Athens and a 19th-century French mining company: ancient ore washeries, the Serpieri shaft and the Kyprianos works.
sights.when: NTUA park hours; washeries open ground. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Keratea NIKE missile base
sights.blurb: The most complete Cold War ruin in Attica: a Greek Air Force NIKE battery under NATO's nuclear umbrella from 1964 to 1989, abandoned in 2005.
sights.when: Open ground; no facilities. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Parnitha 'Aeras' military station
sights.blurb: A disused 1950s antenna post on a Parnitha summit with a gatehouse and twin sentry boxes, burned in 2007.
sights.when: Walk past the barrier. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Penteli NATO station
sights.blurb: Big dishes still standing above Agios Panteleimon: a NATO telecom station that ran until about the late 1990s.
sights.when: Derelict and fenced; outside only. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: German station ruins, Hymettus
sights.blurb: Ruins of a 1942 Luftwaffe signals post near the summit of Hymettus; local writers say the 'radar' was propaganda.

sights.name: US Naval Communications Station, Nea Makri
sights.blurb: A US Navy station built from 1953, mostly underground, closed in 1990 and now a park.

sights.name: Ardittos shelter
sights.blurb: The largest air-raid shelter in Attica (about 1,300 people), under the hill behind the Panathenaic Stadium; three of its four entrances are sealed.
sights.when: Abandoned and closed; the entrance was not located. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Lycabettus shelter
sights.blurb: A c. 1936 shelter cut 100 m into Lycabettus beside the Agioi Isidoroi cave church: larger and better preserved than Ardittos.

sights.name: Praxitelous 33 shelter
sights.blurb: Two reinforced chambers under a late-1930s block, used in the Dekemvriana and opened for a 'Bunker' show.

sights.name: Zalokosta 7 shelter
sights.blurb: An 80 m² basement shelter 50 m from Parliament, in a listed EFKA-owned building.

sights.name: Kastella shelters, Piraeus
sights.blurb: A two-storey abandoned Metaxas-era shelter and a smaller vaulted one on Profitis Ilias hill.
sights.when: Closed or hidden. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: German coastal batteries, Peiraiki
sights.blurb: Empty German gun emplacements on the Peiraiki shore walk; the guns went in 1944.
sights.when: Open coastal walk. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Pillboxes of the Attica coast
sights.blurb: Three intact WWII pillboxes, a naval-gun base and trenches on Porto Rafti's Agios Spyridonas hill; more at Legrena and Varkiza.

sights.name: Elefsina ship graveyard
sights.blurb: Rusting semi-sunk ships against refineries and cement works, 2 km from the Eleusinian sanctuary; much reduced since removals began in 2018.
sights.when: Public shore. Map pin approximate; check how many hulks remain.

sights.name: Korai 4 Kommandantur cells
sights.blurb: Two basement levels 6 m under Syntagma where the Germans held prisoners; their scratched names, planes and ships survive on the walls.
sights.when: Tue–Sat 9:00–14:00, free; closed in August. Tel. 210 324 3581.

sights.name: Merlin 6: the Gestapo house
sights.blurb: A brass relief and an original cell door outside a cosmetics store mark the SS and Gestapo headquarters of 1941–44.

sights.name: Kaisariani Shooting Range
sights.blurb: The wall where the Germans shot 200 communist prisoners on 1 May 1944; they went to their deaths singing.
sights.when: Park open; the memorial enclosure opens irregularly. Memorial plaques vandalised in Feb 2026, repairs promised.

sights.name: Haidari camp, Block 15
sights.blurb: The condemned block of the 'Bastille of Greece', the Haidari camp (1943–44), inside a working army camp.
sights.when: Permit needed; open on commemorations and tour days. Virtual tour: block15.aueb.gr.

sights.name: Kokkinia Blockade Mantra
sights.blurb: The carpet-factory hall where 72 men and 3 women were shot in the Blockade of 17 August 1944; ricochet marks and the old wooden gate survive.

sights.name: Heroon of Faros, Nea Smyrni
sights.blurb: A 1980 bronze where 114 men were shot in August 1944.

sights.name: Nea Smyrni, December 1944
sights.blurb: Plaques of the December 1944 fighting round a refugee suburb: Plateia Skatzouraki, an ELAS hospital, the Iosifogleio orphanage.

sights.name: Beth Shalom and the Holocaust memorial
sights.blurb: The synagogue where Athens's Jews were rounded up on 24 March 1944, and Maganias's broken Star of David nearby.
sights.when: Street; the synagogue by arrangement, with ID.

sights.name: Averof prison stele
sights.blurb: All that marks the Averof prison (1892–1971), demolished in 1972 for the courts; bus 813 still says 'Averof'.

sights.name: Bouboulinas 18
sights.blurb: The junta's Security HQ with its rooftop beating room, demolished just before the junta fell; flats stand there now.

sights.name: Mesogeion 14–18 cells
sights.blurb: The junta's Security headquarters of 1971–74: two original basement cells survive, with plaques since 2017.
sights.when: Government offices; cells open only on special days (17 Nov unconfirmed).

sights.name: EAT-ESA, Parko Eleftherias
sights.blurb: Four low stone buildings in a park where the junta's military police tortured prisoners, including Panagoulis.
sights.when: Park hours; the small museum opens irregularly.

sights.name: Loumbarda, km 31 Athens–Sounio
sights.blurb: The culvert where Panagoulis set his bomb under Papadopoulos's car on 13 August 1968; the junta put up a thanksgiving monument.
sights.when: Roadside on a fast road: dangerous to stop. Monument's survival unknown. Map pin approximate.

sights.name: Panagoulis crash spot
sights.blurb: The metro station named after Panagoulis, near where he died in a suspicious car crash on 1 May 1976.

sights.name: Polytechnic gate, 17 November 1973
sights.blurb: The iron gate crushed by a junta tank on the night of 17 November 1973, kept in the courtyard with a memorial head.

sights.name: Grigoropoulos plaque
sights.blurb: Where the 15-year-old Alexandros Grigoropoulos was shot by a policeman on 6 December 2008, starting weeks of riots.

sights.name: Army Share Fund building
sights.blurb: The block that held the German military administration in 1941–44, now the City Link arcade with Athénée and the Attica store.

sights.name: Kaisariani refugee blocks
sights.blurb: Refugee blocks in 'Little Moscow' with bullet marks from 1944 and a mural.

sights.name: Otto-era guillotine site, Hill of the Nymphs
sights.blurb: Where Edmond About placed the scaffold of King Otto's Athens, below the Observatory.

sights.name: Criminology Museum (last guillotine)
sights.blurb: The last Greek guillotine (used until 1912), bandits' heads in jars and tattooed skin, in the Medical School at Goudi.
sights.when: Appointment only; visitors report calls unanswered and visits refused. Try anyway, by phone.

sights.name: Plateia Lavriou
sights.blurb: A square near Omonia that was the 1889 city terminus of the trains to Kifisia and Lavrio; nothing is left.

sights.name: The open Ilisos at Agia Fotini
sights.blurb: The only stretch of Athens's buried river still open to the sky, where the water of the Kallirroi spring still runs out of two pipes.

sights.name: Hasekis's fountain and konaki
sights.blurb: Built in 1778, the only Ottoman fountain in Athens known to survive, a metre below today's road, with the tyrant Hasekis's mansion behind.
sights.when: Street; the konaki inside the university campus in campus hours.

sights.name: Roman Agora latrines
sights.blurb: A 1st-century public toilet for 64 people sitting side by side over a water channel.

sights.name: Peisistratid aqueduct, Evangelismos
sights.blurb: A section of the 6th-century BC aqueduct of the tyrants shown in Evangelismos metro station.

sights.name: Kilometre zero (and the noon time-ball)
sights.blurb: The Observatory hill, said to be Greece's kilometre zero, where a time-ball once dropped at noon from 1916.
sights.when: Observatory visitor centre evenings; no marker known.

sights.name: Thrasyllos monument sundial
sights.blurb: A metre-wide ancient sundial reported at the Thrasyllos monument above the Theatre of Dionysus, unpublished.
sights.when: Acropolis ticket; seen from the south slope path. Not verified.

sights.name: Profitis Ilias cave, Rizoupoli
sights.blurb: A karst cave in an empty urban plot among apartment blocks.
sights.when: Private plot; see from the street.

sights.name: Medrese gate
sights.blurb: The marble gate of the Ottoman school of 1721, with a rosette and tulip carving; the building behind became a prison and was demolished.

sights.name: The Kolonaki column
sights.blurb: The little ancient column that gave Kolonaki its name, a processional marker against epidemics moved to the square in 1938.
sights.when: Public square; check it is still in place after the redesigns and metro works.

sights.name: The Train at Rouf
sights.blurb: Old railway carriages at Rouf station turned into a theatre, bar and restaurant.

sights.name: Athénée (ex-Zonar's)
sights.blurb: The café of Elytis, Gatsos, Hadjidakis and Karamanlis, in the same building since 1940, reopened in 2015.

sights.name: Dexameni café
sights.blurb: A square café over Hadrian's reservoir where Papadiamantis was photographed with his head tilted; a 1923 relief of him is set into the reservoir wall.
sights.when: Open all day in season, no bookings; open-air Cine Dexameni next door.

sights.name: Mouria corner, Exarchia
sights.blurb: A kafeneio on the same corner since 1915; Mouria itself probably closed on 31 October 2026, but the space is to stay a café.
sights.when: Check on site what is open.

sights.name: Saita, Plaka
sights.blurb: A basement tavern with murals (1970) where songwriter Manolis Rasoulis met Nikos Xydakis in 1978, which led to a landmark album.

sights.name: Galaxy and Adonis, Nea Smyrni
sights.blurb: Where Greek footballers planned their first strike (1979–80) and Panionios's ultras were founded; Adonis is the café of a 1986 hit song.
sights.when: Galaxy is a municipal venue; Adonis is open.

sights.name: Diporto
sights.blurb: A sign-less basement tavern under an abandoned house by the central market, unchanged since the 1950s; no menu.
sights.when: Lunch only, roughly midday to early evening.

sights.name: Klimataria
sights.blurb: A tavern since 1927 where rebetes including Markos Vamvakaris passed through; live music.

sights.name: Oinopoleion, Psyrri
sights.blurb: Psyrri's oldest tavern (1928), where the rebetis Stelios Tsaousakis was a regular in the early 1950s.

sights.name: Brettos, Plaka
sights.blurb: A distillery and bar of 1909 with walls of backlit coloured bottles.

sights.name: Spilia tou Paraskeva, Kastella
sights.blurb: An ancient cave sanctuary (the Serangeion) that became a refreshment stand and then the glamorous 1960s nightclub of Chiotis and Linda; closed in 1968.

sights.name: Ikariotiko kafeneio, Piraeus
sights.blurb: A Piraeus kafeneio since 1945 in a building of the Rizarios foundation.

sights.name: Gennadius Library
sights.blurb: An unchanged 1926 library holding the papers of Seferis, Elytis and Schliemann.
sights.when: Open stacks Sept–June Mon–Wed, Fri 9–16:45, Thu to 19:45, Sat to 13:45; reading room for researchers; public lectures in Cotsen Hall.

sights.name: Vallianeio (old National Library)
sights.blurb: The neoclassical National Library of the 'Athenian trilogy', with its five-storey iron book tower; the reading room's reopening in 2026 is unconfirmed.
sights.when: Reading room closed since late 2023 for ceiling works; reopening 'within 2026' announced, not confirmed.

sights.name: National Library, SNFCC
sights.blurb: Renzo Piano's National Library, open to everyone 9:00–24:00 daily.

sights.name: Parnassos hall
sights.blurb: The 1890–91 hall of the Parnassos literary society, where Coubertin lectured in 1894 and Greece's first art exhibition was held.

sights.name: Athens Conservatory (Despotopoulos)
sights.blurb: Ioannis Despotopoulos's 160 m Bauhaus-trained building (1970s), finished with its 600-seat hall only in 2022.
sights.q: Odeio Athinon, Rigillis and Vas. Georgiou B

sights.name: Hellenic Conservatory, Feidiou 3
sights.blurb: An 1836 Otto-era mansion where Maria Callas studied, derelict for 50 years and being restored as the Dance Archive.
sights.when: Restoration (€5.7m); a 2026 opening was announced, not confirmed. Exterior.

sights.name: Theatro Technis 'Ypogeio'
sights.blurb: Karolos Koun's circular basement theatre (1954), where Beckett, Ionesco and Genet had their Greek premieres.

sights.name: Theatro Technis, Frynichou 14
sights.blurb: Theatro Technis's second stage in Plaka (1985).

sights.name: Rex / Kotopouli stage
sights.blurb: A 1937 cinema-theatre, burned in 1982, listed in 1983, now a National Theatre stage.

sights.name: Aigli Zappeiou
sights.blurb: The open-air cinema in the Zappeion gardens (from the 1900s or 1910s).

sights.name: Cine Thision
sights.blurb: An open-air cinema since 1935 with the Acropolis behind the screen.

sights.name: Cine Paris, Plaka
sights.blurb: A 1920s rooftop cinema in Plaka.

sights.name: Vox and Riviera, Exarchia
sights.blurb: Exarchia's open-air cinemas: Vox (1938) and Riviera (1969).

sights.name: Old Chemistry, Solonos 104
sights.blurb: Ziller's university chemistry lab (1887–90), where a professor hid a Telefunken radio as an 'exhibit' in the Occupation and the 1973 mobilisations began; now the Law Library and a museum of 10,000 scientific instruments.
sights.when: Law Library Mon–Fri 8:30–20:00. Natural Sciences and Technology Museum by arrangement (chsymeon@phys.uoa.gr).

sights.name: Demokritos reactor
sights.blurb: Greece's only nuclear reactor, critical since 31 July 1961, now not operating; a museum is only a plan.
sights.when: Research campus; no public visits found. Exterior only.

sights.name: Newall telescope, Penteli
sights.blurb: A 62.5 cm refractor of 1869, once the largest in the world, in an all-Pentelic-marble building of 1958; public evening shows.
sights.when: Evening shows, about 125 places; book online (noa.gr).

sights.name: Thissio Observatory and Doridis telescope
sights.blurb: Greece's first observatory (1842), founded by Sinas, where Gagarin came in 1962; visitor centre with the Doridis telescope.

sights.name: Hellenic Pasteur Institute
sights.blurb: Founded in 1919 with money from arms dealer Basil Zaharoff and opened by Calmette in 1920; old instruments in cases.

sights.name: Mineralogy and Petrology Museum
sights.blurb: 1,800 specimens of 700+ minerals in 19th-century cases, with a Santorini room, on the Zografou campus.
sights.q: Mouseio Oryktologias kai Petrologias, Panepistimioupoli Zografou

sights.name: Finos Film, Chiou 53
sights.blurb: The listed 1914 soap-factory building where Finos Film made Greek cinema's golden age; about 500 reels were rescued from it in 2021.

sights.name: Rigillis 18
sights.blurb: New Democracy's headquarters 1975–2011, a listed modern monument since 2020, becoming a private home.

sights.name: Agios Ioannis tis Kolonas
sights.blurb: A tiny whitewashed chapel built round an ancient Corinthian column that rises through its roof; Athenians tied fevers to it with threads.
sights.when: Hours conflict: mornings except Sunday (older source) or a monthly liturgy; feast 29 August. The column is visible from Evripidou.

sights.name: Davelis cave and the Pentelic quarry
sights.blurb: Rock-cut Byzantine chapels at the mouth of a cave opened by the ancient quarry that supplied the Parthenon's marble; chisel and wedge marks everywhere.
sights.when: Open air, always; rough road, then a short walk. Cave floor slippery.

sights.name: Omorfokklisia, Galatsi
sights.blurb: An 11th–12th-century church with a Gothic rose on its vault and a famous Pantokrator, open only one day a year.
sights.when: Open only on St George's feast (Easter Monday when it falls in Lent). Otherwise exterior.

sights.name: Little Metropolis (Panagia Gorgoepikoos)
sights.blurb: A tiny church built of about 90 reused ancient and Byzantine carvings, including a frieze of the twelve months and the zodiac.

sights.name: Russian Church (Sotira Lykodimou)
sights.blurb: The largest medieval building in Athens, an 11th-century church given to Russia in 1847, with an aqueduct cistern 5 m under its floor.

sights.name: Megali Panagia, Hadrian's Library
sights.blurb: Foundations of an early-Christian four-apsed church in the courtyard of Hadrian's Library.

sights.name: Panagia Chrysospiliotissa
sights.blurb: A cave chapel in the Acropolis rock above the Theatre of Dionysus, with two ancient columns above it.
sights.when: Seen from the south slope path (Acropolis ticket).
sights.q: Theatre of Dionysus, Acropolis south slope

sights.name: Kapnikarea
sights.blurb: An 11th-century church in the middle of Ermou, saved from demolition by Ludwig of Bavaria.

sights.name: Daphni monastery
sights.blurb: An 11th-century monastery with some of the finest Byzantine mosaics anywhere, including a stern Pantokrator.

sights.name: Kaisariani monastery
sights.blurb: An 11th-century monastery on Hymettus with a spring that runs from a ram's-head spout.

sights.name: Agia Dynami
sights.blurb: An Ottoman-era chapel swallowed by the pilotis of a 1950s ministry block that now stands empty: a church whose sky is the underside of a building.

sights.name: Agioi Isidoroi, Lycabettus
sights.blurb: A 15th–16th-century church built into the largest cave of Lycabettus, with a plaque about a tunnel to Penteli.

sights.name: Catholic Cathedral of St Dionysius
sights.blurb: Klenze's only Athens building (1853–65), with green Tinos-marble columns cut for the royal palace and left over after a redesign.

sights.name: Anglican St Paul's
sights.blurb: A neo-Gothic church of 1843 in bluish-grey Hymettus marble, with the oldest church organ in the city.

sights.name: Agios Konstantinos, Omonia
sights.blurb: Kaftanzoglou's big neo-Byzantine church (1871–1905) near Omonia.

sights.name: Agios Panteleimonas Acharnon
sights.blurb: Called the largest church in Athens, begun in 1910 where a chapel stood for a mother driven mad by grief.

sights.name: Christuskirche, Sina 66
sights.blurb: The German Protestant church of 1931–34 in Neue Sachlichkeit style, with its Bauhaus-era pulpit, pews and candlesticks intact.

sights.name: Romaniote (Ianniotiki) synagogue
sights.blurb: The old synagogue of the Greek-speaking Romaniote Jews, facing Beth Shalom.

sights.name: Metropolitan Cathedral
sights.blurb: The 19th-century cathedral of Athens, with a new treasury museum; next to the Little Metropolis.

sights.name: Agios Dimitrios Loumbardiaris and the Pikionis paths
sights.blurb: Pikionis's 1954–58 landscape of paths, a pavilion and a re-clad chapel, made of marble scraps, tiles and concrete: the masterpiece of Greek modernism.
sights.when: Grounds open; chapel at service times.

sights.name: Koimisi Theotokou, Ano Glyfada
sights.blurb: A modern church designed in 1961 by Molfesis and Papagiannis; whether it was built as drawn is unknown.
sights.when: Parish hours; check what it looks like.

sights.name: Agios Nikolaos, Glyfada
sights.blurb: A 1956–62 church by Paraskevi Tsatiri, a rare woman church architect; the old church was moved for the avenue.

sights.name: Votanikos mosque
sights.blurb: Athens's first official mosque since independence (2020): a state-built, minaret-less building, an 'anti-monument'.
sights.when: Prayer times; ID check at the gate.

sights.name: First Cemetery of Athens
sights.blurb: Athens's great 19th–20th-century cemetery: Halepas's Sleeping Maiden, Schliemann's temple-tomb, cypress avenues.

sights.name: Phaleron War Cemetery
sights.blurb: A Commonwealth war cemetery by Louis de Soissons, sloping to the sea, with Gurkha, Muslim and Crimean plots.

sights.name: German war cemetery, Dionysos
sights.blurb: 9,905 WWII and 68 WWI German dead in 12 crypts under three walled courtyards on Penteli's north slope.

sights.name: Third Cemetery, Nikaia
sights.blurb: The largest cemetery in the Balkans, with Jewish, Italian, Catholic and military sections and the graves of the Kokkinia Blockade victims.

sights.name: Acropolis
sights.blurb: The 5th-century BC sanctuary of Athena: look for the curved steps, the Venetian shell damage of 1687 and the bright new marble of the restorers.
sights.when: Winter 8:00–17:00 (last entry 20 min before); €30 / €15; timed tickets online; free 1st and 3rd Sunday Nov–Mar. Opening slot or last two hours quietest.

sights.name: North Slope: Peripatos and caves
sights.blurb: The quiet side of the Acropolis, reopened in 2025: cave shrines of Apollo, Zeus and Pan, the Klepsydra spring and a boulder that gives the path's length.
sights.when: Enter from inside the Acropolis site (Acropolis ticket). Winter hours conflict (8:30–15:30 vs 8:00–17:00): check on the day.

sights.name: Theatre of Dionysus
sights.blurb: Where tragedy began: look for the priest's throne carved with kneeling Persians holding griffins.

sights.name: Ancient Agora
sights.blurb: The heart of democratic Athens: find the boundary stone that says 'I am the boundary of the Agora', in the first person.
sights.when: From 1 Apr 2026: 8:00–19:30 (winter hours shorter, check hh.gr). About €20 since the combined ticket ended.

sights.name: Roman Agora and Tower of the Winds
sights.blurb: An octagonal marble clock tower of the 1st century BC: sundial lines under each wind, a water clock inside.

sights.name: Kerameikos
sights.blurb: The city's great cemetery and gate, where the Eridanos still flows through the Sacred Gate and carts left ruts on the Pompeion ramp.
sights.when: Reopened 15 Sept 2026 after the upgrade; about €10. Check hours.

sights.name: Olympieion and Hadrian's Arch
sights.blurb: The giant temple finished by Hadrian, with a column felled by a storm in 1852 lying in its drums, and an arch with two inscriptions.

sights.name: Pnyx
sights.blurb: Where the Athenian assembly met: a rock-cut speaker's platform and 58 niches for votives to Zeus Hypsistos. Free.

sights.name: Zea shipsheds through a window
sights.blurb: The slipways of Athens's trireme sheds, seen through the window of an apartment-block basement in Piraeus.

sights.name: Panathenaic Stadium
sights.blurb: The marble stadium of 1896, with a 57 m vaulted tunnel under the bank leading to the torch museum.

sights.name: Areopagus
sights.blurb: The rock of the ancient court where St Paul spoke to the Athenians; a bronze plaque has his speech.
sights.when: Free; slippery steps (2025 works may have changed them).

sights.name: Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
sights.blurb: A dying hoplite copied from an Aegina temple pediment, with Pericles's words; the Evzones change guard on the hour.
sights.q: Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, Syntagma

sights.name: Monastiraki metro: the Eridanos
sights.blurb: Inside the Line 3 station, the Eridanos river still runs in its vaulted Hadrianic channel under a glass walkway; you can hear it.
sights.when: Metro hours, free with a ticket or from the concourse.

sights.name: Syntagma metro: the stratigraphy wall
sights.blurb: A cut through Athens's ground: graves, a foundry, the Peisistratid aqueduct and a 4th-century BC skeleton in the station concourse.

sights.name: Acharnian Gate in the National Bank
sights.blurb: 30 m of the Themistoclean city wall, a gate road with wheel ruts and the moat, 5 m down in a bank's basement.
sights.when: Bank opening hours; ask at the entrance.

sights.name: Kotzia Square dig
sights.blurb: An excavation left open where a car park was never built: three ancient streets, graves and workshops.

sights.name: Elaionas metro bridge
sights.blurb: Piers of what is called the oldest bridge found in Greece, displayed at Elaionas station.

sights.name: Long Walls traces
sights.blurb: Stretches of the walls that tied Athens to Piraeus, visible along Thessalonikis Street and under pilotis near Tavros.

sights.name: Aristotle's Lyceum
sights.blurb: The palaestra of the gymnasium where Aristotle taught walking (the 'Peripatetics').

sights.name: Plato's Academy park
sights.blurb: A neglected park among the ruins of the grove where Plato taught.

sights.name: Hadrian's Library
sights.blurb: Hadrian's great court of books (AD 132), with the foundations of an early church in its garden.

sights.name: Sounion
sights.blurb: The Temple of Poseidon on its cape: look for 'BYRON' and dozens of travellers' names carved into the columns.
sights.when: Go at opening for quiet, at sunset for the view; ticket.

sights.name: Marathon tumulus and museum
sights.blurb: The mound over the Athenian dead of 490 BC, and a museum with Egyptian-style statues from Herodes Atticus's villa.

sights.name: Brauron
sights.blurb: Artemis's sanctuary where Athenian girls served as 'little bears': a 5th-century bridge with wheel grooves, and a temple now 400 m from the silted-up sea.
sights.when: 8:30–15:30, closed Tuesday; site and museum about €5 each.

sights.name: Eleusis
sights.blurb: The sanctuary of the Mysteries, between refineries: find the emperor's bust with a cross scratched into its Gorgon.

offmap.name: Myloi rolling-stock graveyard, Argolida
offmap.blurb: An abandoned junction of the dead Peloponnese metre-gauge network with rusting trains on its sidings, about 2 hours from Athens.
offmap.when: Unverified since 2018; check recent photos before going.

offmap.name: Papanikolaou museum, Kymi (Euboea)
offmap.blurb: The family house of the inventor of the Pap test, now a museum, about 2 hours from Athens.
offmap.when: Short hours (e.g. Tue and Thu evenings, Sat morning); check before going.

offmap.name: Giannakis's Air Force chapel, Kithairon
offmap.blurb: An 'almost anti-plastic' modern chapel built in 1960 by the architect Giannakis on the summit of Kithairon during his military service, near the old NIKE flight.

offmap.name: Ritsona crematorium (Boeotia)
offmap.blurb: Greece's first crematorium (30 Sept 2019), by MONOGON architects, about 80 km from Athens; the end of a long religious and legal fight.

p: A round, three-storey concrete school sits in a grid of ordinary apartment blocks, its southern half wrapped in layered louvred overhangs set to the angle of the sun. Takis Zenetos designed it in 1969–76 so that the classrooms could open into one huge hall; it is his most famous built work and the counterpart of his Lycabettus Theatre.

Zenetos (1926–77) was the visionary of Greek modernism: in 1962 he published 'Electronic Urbanism', a city of floating structures and remote work decades before the internet. Most of his houses have been altered or destroyed; this school, renovated from 2000, is the place where his ideas still stand at full size. The TEE heritage register says he 'broadened the international brutalist code in an imaginative way'.
It is a working school, so look from the street. Walk round the curve to see how the louvres change depth with orientation.
zenetos-school.s: TEE architecture register; archetype.gr; Athens master research (Oct 2026).

p: A long ten-storey slab of raw concrete stands on tall pilotis, with a lower block for the entrance, the dining hall and a 600-seat auditorium. It is the National Technical University's student residence, designed by Papaioannou and Fines around 1967–70 and opened in 1974, and the most complete Corbusian building in Athens.

SOS Brutalism lists it as being in grave danger and says it carries 'almost single-handedly the weight of the country's brutalist architecture'. Maintenance has been minimal for decades; the concrete is stained and patched, which suits the photographs but worries the architects.
Exterior only: the interior is for residents. Combine with the NTUA campus and the Mineralogy Museum in Zografou.

On a quarry ledge on the north-east side of Lycabettus, a ring of seats faces a stage under a light steel roof: Takis Zenetos's theatre of 1965. The actress Anna Synodinou wanted tragedy in the middle of Athens, rented the old quarry from the Petraki monastery and opened the theatre on 12 June 1965 with Antigone.
It closed in 2008 and decayed. A €3.9 million restoration kept Zenetos's design and added new seating; it reopened on 15 September 2023 and is run by the City of Athens for concerts.
The only way in is a ticket for a summer show. The car park beside it has one of the widest views over the basin.

The long white building on Syngrou is the FIX brewery as Takis Zenetos reclothed it in 1957: horizontal bands of glass and brick wrapped round an industrial core from 1864. Half of it was demolished in 1995 for the metro works, and only the two façades he designed were listed. It is now EMST, the National Museum of Contemporary Art.

FIX was the beer of Athens for a century, founded by the Bavarian Fuchs family who came with King Otto. The building's survival in reduced form is a small lesson in how Athens protects modern architecture: by the façade, not the whole.
Go up to the roof bar for the view to the Acropolis. The museum is good on its own terms; the building is the reason it is on this map.

Across from the National Garden, a modernist block by Margaritis Apostolidis and Takis Zenetos (1959–60) has a façade of sliding panels that residents move to open or close their balconies. The building changes face through the day.
The idea was copied, badly and illegally, across thousands of Athenian balconies as aluminium enclosures. Seeing the original explains why so many polykatoikies look the way they do.
Look at it from the garden side of the avenue.

On the steep streets below Lycabettus, a primary school descends the slope in terraces: Pikionis's Pefkakia school of 1931–32. It is the one building in which the architect of the Acropolis paths worked in the pure modernist manner.

Pikionis turned against it almost immediately and spent the rest of his life looking for a Greek modernism rooted in landscape and craft, which led to the Philopappou paths and Agios Dimitrios Loumbardiaris. Seeing the two together shows the turn.
Pin to be checked: Google's match is the 14th Primary School, Sina 70.

In upper Exarchia, Dimitris and Suzana Antonakakis's block (designed 1972–73, built 1974–75) has exposed concrete and a stair that works like a public street running up through the building. Buildings like this are why Tzonis and Lefaivre coined the term 'critical regionalism' in 1981, writing about Greek architects.
Look for the stair from the pavement; that is the point of the building. The Antonakakis also redesigned Kolonaki Square in 2004, since replaced.

A clean early-postwar block near Plateia Mavili: the first work of Nikos Valsamakis, later one of the masters of Greek modernism. Valsamakis himself sent a newspaper photographs of it under construction, sixty years on.
Pair with his other blocks on Vasileos Konstantinou and Irodotou.
One of Nikos Valsamakis's early apartment blocks (1955–56), on a quiet Kolonaki street. Part of a ring of 1950s modernist blocks between Kolonaki and Pangrati.
Valsamakis (1959–60) and, at no. 46, Molfesis (1959) built side by side on Vasileos Konstantinou: two takes on the late-1950s Athenian block facing the National Garden's edge.
A 1959 apartment block by Dimosthenis (Sthenis) Molfesis, next to Valsamakis's no. 42. Molfesis also designed the 1961 church in Ano Glyfada that this map is still trying to find.
Dimitris Papazisis's block (1957–58) shows the better side of the postwar polykatoikia boom: generous halls and a careful façade in an ordinary street.
Early work (1961–62) by the Antonakakis couple with Kostis Gartzos, a decade before their Benaki 118 block. Compare the two to see how their 'street stair' idea developed.
Fatouros and Michailidis's block of 1955: continuous recessed balconies and coloured tile bands at ground level. A postwar answer to the interwar blocks on nearby Fokionos Negri.

Among the neoclassical houses of the Acropolis walk stands a severe modernist house with big openings: Vourekas's design for Xenophon and Lola Zolotas, finished in 1960. Visitors said the Parthenon seemed to come into the living room.
Zolotas was governor of the Bank of Greece and briefly prime minister (1989–90). The house has new owners and was being renovated.

The long white slab at the top of Vasilissis Sofias was the most argued-about building of postwar Athens. Shipowner Apostolos Pezas and Conrad Hilton got the land in 1957; Karamanlis laid the foundation stone in February 1959; the architects were Prokopis Vasileiadis, Emmanouil Vourekas and Spyros Staikos.
Critics called it a skyscraper that would ruin the view; within a decade it was a landmark. The façades carry large incised drawings by the painter Yannis Moralis.

Two glass towers of 25 and 12 storeys at the start of Mesogeion Avenue, by Vikelas and Kymbritis (1971–73). They went up during a short window when the junta relaxed the height limit, and nothing as tall has been allowed in central Athens since.

Twenty-five floors of flats in Ambelokipi, built in 1973 and still the tallest residential building in Greece. It had its own generators and stayed lit through the 1981 and 1999 earthquakes, and once had a rooftop pool bar.

A four-storey brutalist complex begun in 1968 for the junta's broadcaster EIRT and inaugurated in 1974. In June 2013 the government closed ERT overnight; staff occupied the building and broadcast for five months until riot police cleared it on 7 November 2013. It is ERT's headquarters again.

Next to the Nea Filadelfeia grove, 210 workers' flats in two- and three-storey blocks show the frame-and-infill language Konstantinidis later used for his Xenia hotels: bare concrete grid, earthy brick or stone panels. It was his first large commission (1955–57).

He resigned from the Workers' Housing Organisation (OEK) in protest when it pushed for denser building. Residents have since added rooms and enclosed balconies, so look for the blocks that kept the original frame.
oek-filadelfeia.s: TEE register (B46); doma.archi. Map pin approximate.

p: High on Parnitha, Pavlos Mylonas's hotel (1958–61) became a casino in 1971; the hotel itself closed in 1974. The 1972 cable car still climbs to it. Much of the complex is listed. Pair with the Xenia sanatorium ruin and the 'Aeras' station on the same mountain.

Eight long three-storey blocks, 228 flats in all, stand between Alexandras Avenue and the Supreme Court: the refugee housing of 1933–36 for Greeks expelled from Asia Minor and Pontus. Dimitrios Kyriakos designed the four on the avenue, Kimon Laskaris the four behind. They are often called among the first apartment buildings in Greece, Central European functionalism in reinforced concrete with wide courtyards between the slabs.

For decades the state wanted them gone; the Council of State blocked demolition in 2003 and 2009 and the surviving blocks were listed. Many flats are empty or occupied by a residents' collective, others still house descendants of the first families. Bullet marks from December 1944 survive on some walls.
In early 2026 the Attica Region tendered €15 million to restore four blocks as social housing by 2028. Walk the courtyards in daylight and be discreet with the camera: people live here.
prosfygika.s: Athens master research (Oct 2026); Council of State rulings 2003, 2009. Map pin approximate.

p: The blue modernist block over Exarchia Square was designed by Kyriakos Panayotakos in 1932–33, with a colour scheme by the painter Papaloukas. Le Corbusier, visiting for the 1933 CIAM congress that produced the Athens Charter, is reported to have said 'C'est très beau'.
Its ground floor held the café Floral, a left-wing meeting place, until 2016. Today it is one of the best-known images of interwar Athens.

Kypseli was the modern suburb of the 1930s, and Fokionos Negri its showpiece: a long planted boulevard lined with the first modernist apartment blocks. The Lanara block (1938, engineer I. Zolotas) is the best of them, purist with Art Deco touches; its basement served as a shelter in the Occupation.

It was threatened with demolition and listed in 2006. Walk the street from no. 7 (1932, the first modern block here) and no. 9 (Protopapa, 1933) up to here, then turn into Eptanisou for the Bonis shelter block.
lanara.s: Archive of Modern Monuments (eie.gr); Atenistas Kypseli guide; catisart.gr.

protopapa.t: Protopapa block and the first Fokionos Negri blocks
p: No. 7 (N. Papadakis, 1932) and no. 9 (Protopapa, 1933) are the first modern blocks on Fokionos Negri, the start of the 1930s modernist street. Imvrou 22, nearby, is well kept apart from a clumsy added top floor.

Leonidas Bonis designed this block in 1938 for the shipowner Voulgaris, and drew an anti-aircraft shelter into the original plans. It is still there: a central room for 63 people with toilets, a kitchen and working hand-cranked steel doors, documented by urban speleologists in 2014.
Between 1936 and 1940 about 400 public shelters were built in Attica; private ones like this are rarer and better preserved. The shelter is not open; the building is the stop.

Dourgouti was a refugee settlement: the 'Italika' row houses of 1924 and a group of seven interwar blocks survive and now house newer migrants. During the Occupation blockade of 1944 the Armenian quarter here was burned.
dourgouti.s: Myofa PhD thesis; omadaasty.blogspot. Map pin approximate.

p: One of the largest refugee housing estates in Athens: the two-storey houses of 1936 and then 71 apartment blocks, 2,030 flats in all. A good second stop after the Prosfygika for the scale of the 1920s–30s refugee housing effort.

After the 2004 Games the athletes' flats went to workers' housing families, but the administration, retail and sports buildings were abandoned; the admin building was caught up in the Vatopedi land-swap scandal. Graffiti on the fences reads 'Dead Zone'. An abandoned building at the entrance burned on 21 July 2026.

hellinikon.t: Hellinikon: Saarinen terminal and the new park
p: Athens's airport from 1938 to 2001 is now the largest building site in Greece. What is kept tells the old story: Eero Saarinen's East Terminal (designed 1960–69), the control tower, listed hangars, a stretch of runway and the 2004 canoe-slalom course are all to be reused as features of the new Ellinikon park.

After the airport closed, the field lay derelict for two decades with Olympic Airways planes still parked on the apron and the 2004 Olympic venues rotting at its edge. Demolition began in 2020; the Sports Park opened in stages from July 2026, and the Saarinen terminal is meant to become an exhibition building.
The 'abandoned' layer is effectively gone. Come for the terminal's long marble-and-concrete front and the scale of the change; the Experience Centre shows the plans.
hellinikon.s: Protothema (June 2026); Ta Nea, To Vima (July 2026); Architectural Record.

p: A curved stadium of steel and concrete on the Faliro shore, built for the 2004 beach-volleyball tournament, with 9,600 seats round a sand court now turned to weeds. AFP photographed the smashed windows and dust-caked stands in February 2024; it has hosted almost nothing since the Games.

It became the picture editors' shorthand for the cost of 2004. The Attica Region's Aenaon Park plan for the whole Faliro bay would turn the bowl into an open-air amphitheatre; the neighbouring Tae Kwon Do hall was conceded to the Region in January 2026.
Don't climb the fences. The best view is from the coastal promenade and the footbridge.
faliro-volley.s: AFP (Feb 2024); Attica Region Aenaon Park presentation; newmoney.gr (2026). Map pin approximate.

p: Built for Olympic badminton in 2004 and later run as a large theatre, the Goudi hall had a fire on 12 July 2026. What state it is in now was not checked; treat as a lead.
goudi-badminton.s: Protothema headline (Jul 2026). Map pin approximate; not verified.

p: In the pine forest above Melissia stand the concrete wings of a Bauhaus-era sanatorium, balconies turned to the sun for tuberculosis patients. A 1928 decree took about 100 stremmata for it, and it ran as the 'Penteli Sanatorium' from 1930, later as the IKA hospital until 2016. Since then it has been stripped and burned.

Penteli's dry air made it the 'Greek Davos': several sanatoria went up on its slopes between the wars. The Daou sanatorium nearby was a resistance hideout, the Bobolas wing and the Naval Sanatorium decay in the same woods.
Visitors in reviews mention vagrants and broken glass; keep to the outside. A redevelopment as a health park has been announced more than once (plans of 52 to 75 stremmata).
papadimitriou-sanatorium.s: virus.com.gr; vrilissianews.gr; adarch.gr; Athens Social Atlas.

p: Above the Rafina crossroads, a stone-built sanatorium stands roofless in the pines. Its staff were members of ELAS during the Occupation and it served as a hideout; a nurse was executed in 1944.

On the Mont Parnes road, a long ruin with empty window rows: a 1930s sanatorium, then an EOT Xenia hotel, then a tourism school that closed in 1980. The 1999 earthquake damaged it further. Urban explorers call it the most visited ruin in Greece. Pair with the 'Aeras' station and the casino.

Next to Larissa station stands the old terminus of the metre-gauge network to the Peloponnese (Athens–Corinth from 1885), which from 1929 also ran the Lavrio trains. It closed in 2005; the whole metre-gauge Peloponnese network has been suspended since 2011.
spap-station.s: Athens master research (Oct 2026). Map pin approximate.

p: Founded in 1909, the Lipasmata (fertiliser) works grew to about 250,000 m² and 109 buildings on the Drapetsona shore, one of the largest chemical plants in Europe. Most was demolished around 2003; what was kept now stands in a public park: the power station, the glass-works chimney and silo, the water tower, the chemistry institute, the Krakari conveyor gantry.

For a chemist it is a lesson in the Haber-era fertiliser industry and its cost: the plant was notorious for pollution and for its workers' strikes. The park's own site says it closed in 1993; other sources say 1999.
Walk the full seafront path from the north entrance to Krakari; ships for Piraeus pass close.
The textile giant's Megalo Pefko mill opened in 1950 as the first new factory of the postwar recovery; Time praised it in 1962. It closed in 1992 and stands empty on the road to Megara.

On the slopes of Parnitha, George I bought Tatoi in 1872 and the royal family spent summers here among farms, stables, vineyards and forest. After the monarchy was abolished in 1974 the estate decayed for decades; the 2021 Parnitha fire burned up to the royal cemetery, whose mausoleum and church survived.

A €70 million Culture Ministry project is turning the historic core into three museums; about 4,350 objects are to be shown in the palace, out of more than 100,000 recovered and conserved. Princess Irene was buried here in January 2026.
The landscape cemetery in the woods is the stop for this map. Reports in October 2026 put the opening in December.
tatoi.s: To Vima English (2026); Greek City Times (Oct 2026); Neos Kosmos (Jan 2026).

p: A bare island 2.5 nautical miles off Lavrio held political prisoners from 1946–47 to the late 1950s; up to about 100,000 passed through (a high estimate), among them Mikis Theodorakis and Yannis Ritsos. Repentant inmates were made to build copies of classical monuments. In the massacre of the First Sapper Battalion (29 Feb–1 Mar 1948), guards killed an estimated 350 prisoners.
It was declared a historic site in 1989. What remains are foundations, camp buildings and small churches on a dry ridge, and the silence.

Sotiria was Athens's great tuberculosis hospital. In 1936 Georgakopoulos and Despotopoulos (later the architect of the Athens Conservatory) designed its kitchen, laundry and dormitory building and the 'Mega Laikon' hospital wing, listed among the key modern works in Greece. Which buildings stand unaltered is still to be checked.
sotiria.s: Giamarelos (UCL, 2016) list of key works; Despotopoulos biography (Benaki). Map pin approximate; not verified.

p: The brick halls and red-and-white chimney on the Keratsini waterfront are the Agios Georgios power station, which made electricity for Athens from 1928. Locals call it the Drakos, the dragon. In October 1944 ELAS fighters held it against the retreating Germans, who meant to blow it up: the 'Battle of the Electric', remembered by an exhibition inside since 2017.
The historic plant stopped producing in 2012 (efsyn, Parliament); two later gas units stayed on reserve. In 2023 the Environment Ministry listed the historic buildings, façades and the chimney.
Pair with the Lipasmata park a short walk south and the Faliro station for the full story of Athens's electricity.
keratsini-ps.s: efsyn.gr; avgi.gr; VI.D.A. archive; ΦΕΚ 2023 listing. Map pin approximate.

p: Built in 1903 to power the electric railway and the city, the Neo Faliro station was the first large thermal plant in Greece. It ran as a reserve until 1972, was listed in 1986 and became a PPC training school in part; the historic hall stands derelict.
Art shows have used the ruined wing: composer Dimitris Kamarotos once hung an electric guitar from the roof as a giant pendulum. A 1940s pipeline linked it to Keratsini.
faliro-ps.s: lifo.gr; vida-omada; filoibenaki.gr; oneman.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: One of the 'ghost factories' of Pireos Street: CHROPEI made paints from 1899 to 1989; the listed complex passed to the Development Ministry in 2019 and stands empty. IVI and other works nearby are in the same state.
A 28,000 m² former industrial complex with ten listed concrete buildings, the Athens Festival's summer venue. The Culture Ministry plans a permanent conversion.

Athens had no reliable water until the 1920s. The Ulen contract (1924) brought the Marathon dam, inaugurated in 1929 and faced in white marble over a core of crushed-marble concrete with volcanic ash, and the 13.4 km Boyati tunnel that carried the water to Galatsi; about 450 men worked on the tunnel round the clock until 1931.
The dam is the only one in the world clad in marble. Ulen's 35 mm construction film survives. The small EYDAP museum by the crest tells the story.
marathon-dam.s: eydap.gr; el.wikipedia (Ulen); marathonpress.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: The Attica Railways line to Lavrio carried passengers until 1957 and was abolished in 1962. At Thorikos rails, a railway bridge at the fishing-shelter entrance and a decaying station remain; the small Daskaleio station has been restored, and rails resurface on Mesogeia roads (local report, Nov 2026).
lavrio-line.s: el.wikipedia; tanea.gr; lavriaki.gr (Nov 2026). Map pin approximate.

p: The silver that paid for the fleet at Salamis came from Lavrio. In the Souriza valley and at Thorikos you can walk among ancient ore washeries, flat and helical tables where water separated galena (lead sulphide) from the rock and was recycled through cisterns.

In the 1860s Italian and French companies reopened the mines to work the ancient slag. Their works at Kyprianos are now the NTUA Technological and Cultural Park; the Serpieri shaft stands at Kamariza; an 1888 iron ore-loading bridge reaches into Lavrio port.
A full day with the mineralogical museum in Lavrio town; combine with Thorikos theatre and the Keratea missile base.
lavrio-mines.s: ltcp.ntua.gr; lavrioguide.gr; oryktosploutos.net. Map pin approximate.

p: On a hill near Keratea lie the launch pads, bunkers and control buildings of a NIKE surface-to-air missile battery. The Greek Air Force formed 350 Squadron in 1960 with four flights: Keratea, Hymettus, Parnitha and Kithairon. It joined NATO's nuclear role in 1964; nuclear warheads were held by a small US custody detachment.
The nuclear role ended in January 1989 and the unit moved to Sedes in 2005, leaving Keratea empty. Of the four Attica sites it is the only one documented and accessible.
Drone footage shows the layout well; on the ground, look for the missile magazines and the separate radar hill.
keratea-nike.s: haf.gr via parapolitika.gr; irafina.gr; newsbeast.gr; Nike Historical Society. Map pin approximate.

p: A gatehouse with twin sentry boxes, burned-out buildings and antenna bases on one of Parnitha's summits, abandoned for over 25 years and burned in the 2007 fire. The view takes in the whole basin.

Past Agios Panteleimon on Penteli, large dishes and looted buildings mark a military telecom station that served NATO communications until about the late 1990s. It was probably part of ACE High, NATO's chain of 'troposcatter' stations that bounced radio off the lower atmosphere from Norway to Turkey.

Local stories say it relayed Scandinavian signals to the US, and a BBC piece repeated the claim that NATO took Pentelic marble for satellites: folklore, but good folklore. Whether this is one site or two with the military works near the Davelis cave is unresolved.
penteli-nato.s: irafina.gr; newsbeast.gr. Map pin approximate; not verified.

p: Just north of trig point 827 on Hymettus, next to the last OTE mast, are the foundations of a German 40th Signals Regiment post of 1942. Locals call it the German radar; local writers think the radar was a story the Germans spread.

navcommsta.t: US Naval Communications Station, Nea Makri
p: At Brexiza, the US Navy built a communications station from 1953, mostly underground. It closed in 1990 and was handed back in 2004; it is now an athletic and cultural park. How much of the underground part survives is unchecked.

Inside Ardittos hill runs the largest shelter in Attica, for about 1,300 people. Sources disagree on its origin: Skai says the Germans built it in 1943–44; others say it was a prewar air-defence coordination centre that the Germans took over as an ammunition store, used by the resistance afterwards.
Three of its four entrances have been sealed by building; the one left makes it unsafe. Its exact entrance is not public. Stand on the hill above the stadium and imagine the tunnels below.
ardittos-shelter.s: skai.gr; protothema.gr; parapolitika.gr. Map pin approximate; not verified.

p: Around 1936 a shelter was cut about 100 metres into the rock of Lycabettus, next to the cave church of Agioi Isidoroi, with two entrances. Reports describe it as bigger and in better condition than the Ardittos shelter. It is closed; visit the cave church and look for the sealed openings.
lycabettus-shelter.s: parapolitika.gr; in.gr; aftodioikisi.gr (Mar 2026). Map pin approximate.

p: Under a late-1930s modernist block, two reinforced chambers with steel-shuttered vents survive. They were used during the December 1944 fighting and opened to the public for an art show called 'Bunker'.
A basement shelter of about 80 m² in a listed building 50 metres from Parliament, reported in good condition. Closed; a pass-by stop on the way to Kolonaki.
Piraeus was bombed hard in 1941–44. On Kastella a two-storey Metaxas-era shelter stands abandoned, and a smaller one with stone walls and a concrete barrel vault lies on Profitis Ilias hill.
Along the rocky Peiraiki coast, concrete emplacements of German coastal batteries survive empty; the guns were removed in 1944.

The best preserved of Attica's coastal fortifications: three intact pillboxes, a gun base and trenches on the hill above Porto Rafti. A graffitied pillbox at Legrena (reported Aug 2026) and a neglected beach pillbox at Varkiza complete the set.
porto-rafti-pillboxes.s: skai.gr; lavriaki.gr; mixanitouxronou.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: For decades the Gulf of Elefsina was where Greece left its dead ships; AP called it 'an environmental bomb'. The state began removing hulks in 2018, so what remains in 2026 is uncertain. Combine with the sanctuary of Eleusis.
elefsina-wrecks.s: AP; Athens master research (Oct 2026). Map pin approximate.

p: Six metres under a smart office building off Panepistimiou, a 1938 gas-proof shelter of the National Insurance company became the cells of the German Kommandantur. The prisoners' graffiti has been conserved: names, dates, calendars, drawings of planes and ships, even a small Hitler portrait, scratched into doors and plaster. The outlines of the isolation cells are marked on the floor.
People were held here for anything from resistance to 'stealing bread' or climbing on a tram. From here many went on to Haidari.
Free and rarely busy. The man at the desk answers questions; little is in English, so read up before.
korai-4.s: Korai 4 Memorial Site; in.gr; Google Places (hours).

p: Next to the entrance of a Hondos Center store stands Thanasis Apartis's relief of a bound, naked man with a noose and the words 'This used to be the Gestapo hellhole 1941–1944'. The house was demolished in 1980; the iron cell door kept in the memorial is all that survives of it.
This was the SS and Gestapo interrogation centre; prisoners went on to Haidari. A historian of the Occupation told AFP in 2024 that in another European country this would be a museum.

On 1 May 1944 the Germans shot 200 communist prisoners here in batches of twenty, in reprisal for the killing of a German general. Most were long-term prisoners from Akronauplia brought from Haidari. Eyewitnesses describe them singing as they walked to the wall. A black granite memorial lists the names inside what is now a park with a café and playground.

In February 2026 twelve unseen photographs of the condemned surfaced on eBay; the Culture Ministry declared them a protected monument, and within hours vandals smashed the memorial plaques. The municipality promised to repair and upgrade the site.
Weizsäcker came here in 1987; Tsipras made it his first stop as prime minister in 2015. The National Resistance Museum is nearby.
kaisariani-range.s: Greek City Times (Feb 2026); Atlas Obscura; Athens master research (Oct 2026).

p: Over 21,000 people passed through Haidari between September 1943 and September 1944, including Jews deported to Auschwitz; a former inmate estimated some 2,000 executions. Block 15 was the solitary and condemned block, the start point for the 200 of Kaisariani. It was listed in 1987 and is decaying inside an active camp.
haidari-block15.s: Hellenic Ministry of National Defence; block15.aueb.gr; D2 (Nov 2026).

p: On 17 August 1944 German troops and Security Battalions sealed Kokkinia (Nikaia), herded the men into the square and had hooded informers pick out resistance members. Those chosen were shot in this walled factory yard, the Mantra: 72 men and 3 women. The Blockade's total dead is given as over 200 (Attica Region) to 315 (Wikipedia).

The hall keeps ricochet marks in the walls and the wooden gate, the 'Portara', listed as a monument. Inside, a portrait of almost every victim. Celtic-cross graffiti was sprayed on it in September 2024.
Visitors call it one of the most moving museums in Athens. Pair with Plateia Osias Xenis (the selection point) and the Third Cemetery, where the dead are buried.
Kantzilieris's bronze of 1980 stands where 114 men were executed in August 1944. The exact wall is not identified in the sources found.

Nea Smyrni, built for refugees from Smyrna, saw heavy fighting in December 1944. A local walk links the plaque on Plateia Skatzouraki, the ELAS hospital at Korai and Sofouli, and the 1920s Iosifogleio orphanage on Syngrou, requisitioned in 1941.

beth-shalom.t: Beth Shalom and the Holocaust memorial
p: On Friday 24 March 1944 the Germans used the regular registration at the Beth Shalom synagogue to arrest the Jews of Athens; most were deported to Auschwitz. The Community gives 23 March; the 1947 plaque says 24. Across the street is the old Romaniote synagogue.
A few minutes away, Dimitris Maganias's Holocaust memorial (2010) is a Star of David broken into pieces, each pointing to a Greek Jewish community. The Jewish Museum on Nikis tells the rest.
beth-shalom.s: tovima.gr; maxmag; Jewish Museum of Greece.

p: The Averof prison held political prisoners for eighty years, from the Metaxas years to the junta. It was demolished in 1972 and the courts built on the site; a stele in the courtyard and the name on the 813 bus are what remain.

Bouboulinas 18, once a clinic and a hotel, was the Security Police headquarters of the junta until 1971; prisoners were beaten on the soles of the feet (falanga) in a room on the roof. It was demolished shortly before the junta fell, and a block of flats stands on the site.
Next door, nos. 20–22 (the Logothetopoulos building, now a Culture Ministry office) is often wrongly pointed out as the torture building. In 1971 the Security moved to Mesogeion 14–18.

When the Security Police left Bouboulinas in 1971, they moved here, to a 1960 office block now used by the General Secretariat for Research and Innovation. Two original basement cells survive. Plaques at the entrance and in the basement have marked them since November 2017.
Historian Kallivretakis documented the building for the National Hellenic Research Foundation in 2019. Whether the cells open around 17 November was not confirmed.

In what is now Freedom Park, behind the US Embassy, four low buildings were the Special Interrogation Section of the Military Police (EAT-ESA), the junta's worst torture centre. Alexandros Panagoulis was held and beaten here after his attempt on Papadopoulos in 1968. A small anti-dictatorship memorial occupies one building.

On 13 August 1968 Alexandros Panagoulis detonated a bomb in a 7 m culvert under the coast road as the dictator Papadopoulos drove by; it missed. The junta put up a monument 'in remembrance', paid for by the 32nd Marines. Whether it still stands is unknown.
loumbarda.s: mixanitouxronou.gr; mesogianews. Map pin approximate; not verified.

p: Panagoulis survived torture and prison, became an MP and was investigating junta files when he died in a car crash on Vouliagmenis Avenue on 1 May 1976. Many still consider it suspicious. The metro station carries his name.

On 14 November 1973 students occupied the Polytechnic and broadcast against the junta from a radio in the building. In the early hours of the 17th a tank drove through the main gate. The twisted gate is preserved in the courtyard beside the memorial; a bronze head lies on the ground.
Every 17 November a march goes from here to the US Embassy, and the gate is covered in flowers. Enter from Stournari on ordinary days.

A marble plaque and an informal shrine at Tzavella and Mesologgiou mark where a special guard shot Alexandros Grigoropoulos on 6 December 2008. The killing set off the largest riots in Greece in decades.

The Army Share Fund building (listed 1994) was the seat of the German military administration during the Occupation. Today it is the City Link complex, home to Athénée (ex-Zonar's) and the Attica department store, which stands on the site of Flokas café.
Kaisariani, a refugee suburb called 'Little Moscow' for its resistance, keeps bullet-marked refugee blocks and a mural. Walk here after the Shooting Range.

guillotine-nymphs.t: Otto-era guillotine site, Hill of the Nymphs
p: The guillotine came to Greece with the Bavarians. In 'La Grèce contemporaine' (1854) Edmond About places executions near the Cave of the Nymphs below the Observatory hill. Nothing marks the spot; the last guillotine itself is in the Criminology Museum.
guillotine-nymphs.s: vradini; insider.gr; About (1854). Location not verified.

p: In the Athens Medical School at Goudi, the Criminology Museum keeps the last guillotine used in Greece (last on 11 April 1912), the preserved heads of 19th-century bandits, tattooed skin, embryos in formalin and murder weapons from old cases.
Getting in is the hard part: Google reviews in 2026 say the phone goes unanswered and requests are refused. Worth one call.

From 1889 the metre-gauge Attica Railways started here for Kifisia, Strofyli and Lavrio. Bus owners lobbied the line to death in 1957. No trace survives that the research found: a stop for the story only.

ilisos-open.t: The open Ilisos at Agia Fotini
p: Below the church of Agia Fotini, a short rocky bed is the last piece of the Ilisos still open. The rest of Plato's river, where Socrates sat with Phaedrus, runs 6–7 m under Kallirrois Avenue since the Metaxas government covered it in the late 1930s.
Look for two pipes where the water of the ancient Kallirroi spring still comes out. The underground channel has been damaged at Tavros since 2018.

Hadji Ali Hasekis ruled Athens brutally in the 1770s–80s; he built the city wall named after him and, in 1778, this fountain fed from the Glykotrypa springs, with double-curved arches. Ta Nea calls it the only surviving fountain of Ottoman Athens. It sits about a metre below the modern road.
Behind it, in the Agricultural University campus, his country house (konaki) keeps a vaulted ground floor and a wall fragment inside the later 'Krimbas' building.

At the east edge of the Roman Agora, a square room had seats for 64 over a channel of running water, with a gutter at their feet. Romans talked here; nobody had a cubicle. Look from the fence by the Tower of the Winds.

Found during the metro works, a section of the terracotta-lined aqueduct of the Peisistratid tyrants (6th century BC) is displayed in Evangelismos station. Other metro stations (Syntagma, Panepistimio, Dafni) show more of the city's water history.

Aggregator sites say Greece's road distances are measured from the Observatory courtyard; no physical marker has been found. The Observatory also had a noon time-ball from 1916 so the city could set its clocks. Both are leads to check on site.

A blog author reports a large, unpublished sundial (about 1 m) by the choregic monument of Thrasyllos, the cave front above the Theatre of Dionysus. Whether it is displayed or stored is unknown: a find-it detail for the south-slope walk.
A natural karst cave opens in an empty plot in Rizoupoli, surrounded by flats; newsbomb reported it in 2026. Private land: look from outside.

All that stands of the medrese (religious school) founded by Mehmet Fahri in 1721 is its marble gateway, with an Ottoman Turkish inscription of the Tulip Period, a rosette and a tulip. After independence the building became a prison where executions took place, until it was pulled down in 1915.
It stands in the shadow of Hadrian's Library and the Fethiye mosque. Read the inscription with an app: it names the benefactor and the year 1133 AH.

A short marble column about 2 m high, found near Dexameni, was a medieval marker of processions against the plague; it gave the district its name ('little column'). It was moved to the square in 1938. The square has been redesigned since and a metro station is being built: check it is still there.
At the old Rouf station on the Peloponnese line, a set of historic carriages works as a theatre, restaurant and bar. A pleasant end to a western-Athens day.

Zonar's opened in this building on 23 August 1940 (the founder Karolos Zonaras, a Greek-American, had started elsewhere in 1934 or 1939; sources disagree). For four decades it was where Athens was seen: Elytis, Gatsos, the painter Ghikas, Hadjidakis (who gave a French TV interview here with Melina Mercouri), Karezi, Kambanellis, Karamanlis; Durrell and Borges passed through.

Two of its waiters turned up in Nazi uniform in 1941, having been fifth-column spies. Seferis found it 'badly lit and vulgarly furnished'. It closed in 2001, reopened, closed again, and was renovated by K-Studio as Athénée in 2015.
The claim that Sartre and de Beauvoir 'had their table' comes from renovation PR: treat it as marketing.

Plateia Dexamenis sits on top of the reservoir built by Hadrian and still in use. At the start of the 20th century this was the 'hermitage' of Alexandros Papadiamantis, who sat here with Varnalis, Sikelianos and Souris; the famous photo of him with his head on one side was taken here, and a 1923 relief of him is set into the reservoir masonry.
Today's café is a renovated successor (reopened 2012) of the old kafeneia of Barbayiannis and 'Terpsi'. The links to Kazantzakis and Elytis are thinner; Elytis has had a statue here since 1997.

Licensed in 1915 and named after a mulberry tree, Mouria moved from a shack to a two-storey house and in 1962 into the ground floor of the block on the same corner of Charilaou Trikoupi and Kallidromiou. Plays, book launches and political meetings were held here; no famous regulars are well sourced.

In 2026 the landlord planned a pharmacy; a petition passed 7,500 signatures. In July the owner's daughter said the space would stay a café 'but we don't know if it will be Mouria'. The Mouria business is reported closed from 31 October 2026.

A family-run basement taverna since 1970. Here in 1978 Manolis Rasoulis met Nikos Xydakis, which led to 'I ekdikisi tis gyftias', one of the defining Greek albums. Savvopoulos was a regular (the owners say). A guide's claim that Seferis was 'in this house' in 1944 doesn't fit a 1970 business.

At Galaxy, top-division footballers met in 1979–80 before their first big strike, and the Panionios 'Panthers' ultras were founded one winter night in 1983. Galaxy closed in 2001 and is a municipal venue now. Adonis, made famous by Kraounakis's 1986 song sung by Protopsalti, still operates, renovated.

Down a few steps under a derelict 150-year-old house by the Central Market, Diporto has no sign and no menu: you eat what was cooked that day, among barrels, with market workers. The interior is said to be unchanged since the 1950s.
The story that Varnalis wrote 'The Moirai' here is folklore. A rumour that it was closing was denied by the co-owner.
A taverna on Plateia Theatrou since 1927, near the market, with live rebetiko and laiko. Markos and other rebetes are recorded as passing through.
The oldest tavern in Psyrri, from 1928, reopened in 2011. The rebetiko singer Tsaousakis was a regular in the early 1950s.
A Plaka distillery since 1909, now a bar whose walls of coloured bottles glow from behind. No documented famous regulars; on the map for the room.

At Votsalakia on the Kastella shore, a cave in the rock was an ancient sanctuary and bath, the Serangeion, found in 1897. In the 1920s it held a refreshment stand; by the 1960s it was the Spilia tou Paraskeva nightclub, where Manolis Chiotis and Mary Linda played and Onassis, Callas and Grace Kelly are said to have come.
The junta's mayor closed it in 1968 and it has been fenced ever since. A link with 'Never on Sunday' is claimed by one tourism site only and was not confirmed.
Stand on the shore road and look in through the fence; the Sunday stroll from Piraeus to 'the Paraskeva' is an old local habit.
A port kafeneio running since 1945, in a building owned by the Rizarios foundation; one of several old cafés of Piraeus that LiFO lists as survivors.

The American School's Gennadius Library opened in 1926 in a marble building that has not changed. It holds the archives of Seferis and Elytis and the papers of Tsatsos, Venezis, Terzakis, Myrivilis and Schliemann. No source shows Seferis worked in the reading room: this is 'sit among their papers', not 'where they sat'. The easy way in is a lecture.

The middle building of the 'trilogy' on Panepistimiou (Hansen's design, built 1887–1902) was the National Library until the move to the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Centre. Its reading room has a coffered ceiling and a five-storey cast-iron book stack in the tower behind.
The reading room has been closed since the end of 2023 for work on the ceiling; parapolitika reported it would reopen to the public in 2026. Check before going.
The new National Library in Renzo Piano's Stavros Niarchos centre: reading rooms open to anyone from 9 in the morning until midnight. Climb to the lighthouse roof for the view.

The Parnassos Literary Society's building on Plateia Karytsi has a grand hall with Roilos's painting 'The Poets'. Here Pierre de Coubertin spoke on 4 November 1894, campaigning for the first modern Olympics; Greece's first art exhibition was held under the society in 1885; in the Occupation a German military court sat here.
The society admitted its first women members only in 2023. Watch for a lecture or concert to get in.

A long low white building on Rigillis is the Athens Conservatory, designed by Ioannis Despotopoulos, who trained at the Bauhaus, as part of an unbuilt cultural centre (1959–67). Building began in 1970 and the Conservatory (founded 1871) moved in in 1977; the 600-seat amphitheatre opened only on 12 December 2022. It has been a listed modern monument since 2017.
Correction: it is often credited to Fatseas; the architect is Despotopoulos. The tree-filled garden in front is getting a €3.18 million redesign.

Built in 1836 for the Austrian diplomat Prokesch von Osten, this is one of the oldest houses outside the old town. From 1919 it housed Kalomiris's Hellenic Conservatory, where Maria Callas and Nana Mouskouri studied. It stood empty for about 50 years, burned, and in July 2022 part of its south wall collapsed onto the Ideal cinema next door.
The Culture Ministry took it over and is restoring it as the home of the Dance Archive of Greece; it was listed among the 2026 openings.

In a basement off Stadiou, Karolos Koun opened his round theatre in 1954. Here Athens first saw Beckett, Ionesco and Genet, and a generation of actors and directors learned their trade. It is still the Theatro Technis main stage; buy a ticket to sit where Koun's audience sat.
Koun's company's second stage, opened in 1985 in Plaka.
