The Rex opened in 1937 as a large cinema and theatre complex; after a fire in 1982 it was listed and restored, and it is now the National Theatre's Kotopouli stage, named after the actress Marika Kotopouli.
One of the classic open-air summer cinemas, in the Zappeion gardens; its start date is given as 1903 or the late 1910s.
Since 1935, summer films on Apostolou Pavlou with the lit Acropolis behind the screen.
A Plaka roof-terrace cinema dating from the 1920s, with the Acropolis in view.
Vox on Exarchia Square dates from 1938; Riviera on Valtetsiou opened in 1969, run by the Riggas family, who also ran Vox and the Athinaia.

This is the building for a chemist. Ernst Ziller designed the University's chemistry laboratory with advice from August Wilhelm von Hofmann; at the foundation on 6 June 1887 a glass cylinder with a gold coin and a dedication 'to scientific work' was laid under it. Anastasios Christomanos founded chemistry teaching here; Carathéodory, Hondros and Zervas taught in its great amphitheatre. It burned in 1911 and was rebuilt by 1918; it also held the General Chemical Laboratory of the State and the national weights-and-measures office.

In the Occupation professor Caesar Alexopoulos hid a Telefunken transmitter by displaying it as a teaching exhibit; an antenna is still on the roof. In November 1973 the student mobilisations against the junta started here before moving to the Polytechnic.

Since 2017 it is the Law School Library (restored with SNF funds), with original benches and one laboratory preserved. Upstairs the University's Museum of Natural Sciences and Technology keeps more than 10,000 instruments, a Telefunken telegraphy collection and the archive of the University of Smyrna that Carathéodory saved in 1922. The story that Greece's national metre and kilogram copies were kept here is unproven.

In the pines of Agia Paraskevi, the Demokritos research centre's 'swimming-pool' reactor, supplied by AMF Atomics in 1957, went critical on 31 July 1961, Greece's entry into the atomic age; it ran at 5 MW from 1971 and made medical isotopes such as I-131 and Tc-99m.
It is no longer operating. A museum has been proposed, with the blue Cherenkov glow of the pool as the dream exhibit, but no visits were found. Open days at Demokritos are the chance.

The Newall refractor was built in 1869 for a British amateur and for a few years was the largest in the world. It worked at Cambridge until 1957 and came to Penteli in 1959, housed in a building made entirely of Pentelic marble, with a moving floor so visitors can reach the eyepiece. Scientific use ended in the mid-1980s.
The National Observatory runs evening shows with a talk and, weather permitting, a look through the telescope.

The National Observatory's first building on the Hill of the Nymphs (Hansen, 1842), paid for by Baron Sinas; Schmidt and Eginitis worked here and Yuri Gagarin visited in February 1962. The visitor centre opens in the evenings with the historic Doridis telescope.
Leads to look for on site: the kilometre zero and the noon time-ball.

Basil Zaharoff, the Anatolian-Greek arms dealer, paid for the Hellenic Pasteur Institute, opened in March 1920 by Albert Calmette of BCG fame. Historic instruments stand in cases by the amphitheatre; groups can book tours (Friends of the Benaki have run them).
The University's mineral collection: about 1,800 specimens of over 700 mineral species in old wooden cases, plus a room on the Santorini volcano. Look for Lavrio minerals before a trip there.

In 1954 Filopimin Finos moved his company into the old Papoutsanis soap factory at Chiou 53, near Larissa station. Here the films of Greek cinema's golden age were developed, edited and mixed; the building appears in the 1966 film 'Pente chiliades psemata'. It was listed in 1986 and carries a plaque.

Film labs worked here until 2012. In July 2021 about 500 reels, including Angelopoulos's 'The Weeping Meadow', were taken out of the basement by the Greek Film Centre after a reported chemical leak (which people who knew the building denied). The building has been for sale.
Finos's stages were first at 'Atlantis' on Liosion Street, by a cement works, then from 1958 in the old Merlas stables at Agioi Anargyroi.
Karamanlis's party had its headquarters here from 1975 to 2011. The building was declared a modern monument in 2020 and a 2025 permit turns it into a private residence.

Among the spice shops of Evripidou, behind railings and trees, a single-cell chapel encloses a Roman Corinthian column whose capital pokes out of the roof. The church was built round it; a basilica here is dated to 565 by one source, and the present chapel is much later. The site is thought to have been a sanctuary of Asklepios: a mosaic floor and six ancient wells were found in 1917.

The healing tradition survived the change of god. Until the 20th century Athenians with malaria tied red and white threads to the column to bind the fever; legend said diseases were buried beneath it.

Treasure-hunt clue: find the capital above the roof among the branches, then the column inside the sanctuary. Atlas Obscura says the Eridanos runs under the church and can be heard after rain: unverified.
ag-ioannis-kolona.s: churchesingreece.blogspot (2013); Atlas Obscura; Spotted by Locals; pemptousia; avgi.

davelis-cave.t: Davelis cave and the Pentelic quarry
p: At about 700 m on the south-west face of Penteli, the ancient Spilia quarry cut so deep that it opened a cave. The quarry faces still show the ancient chisel and wedge marks, and a paved sledge path down which blocks for the Parthenon were dragged is partly preserved. In the cave mouth two small chapels, Agios Spyridon and Agios Nikolaos, are cut into the rock; their 1233–34 frescoes were moved to the Byzantine Museum in 1981.

The cave is named after Davelis, a 19th-century brigand, and has gathered legends: Pan worship, monks, Cold War tunnels. Wikipedia notes there is no evidence of Pan worship here; the shrine of Pan and the Nymphs is a smaller cave about 800 m up the slope, excavated in 1952. Military works around 1970 damaged the site.
Treasure-hunt clue: put your hand in a wedge slot. For a chemist, this is calcite marble with its famous slight iron content, which turns the Parthenon honey-coloured.
davelis-cave.s: en.wikipedia; penteli.gov.gr; odysseus.culture.gr; Google Places visitor notes.

p: Opposite the Veikou grove, the 'beautiful church' of St George is a cross-in-square of the 11th–12th century on earlier foundations, with a 13th–14th-century chapel and a later narthex. Its 13th-century frescoes include the martyrdom of St George on the wheel and a dome Pantokrator that Fotis Kontoglou called one of the most beautiful in the Christian East.

It is locked all year except on St George's day, when it fills with people. Treasure-hunt clue: a Gothic rose on the western cross-vault, a Frankish touch in a Byzantine church, and pilgrims' prayers scratched into the plaster.
omorfokklisia.s: Protothema (2024); Orthodoxia News Agency (2024); en.wikipedia; ertnews.

p: Next to the big 19th-century cathedral sits the tiny Panagia Gorgoepikoos (also Agios Eleftherios), built almost entirely of spolia: about 90 carved blocks from ancient, early Christian and middle Byzantine buildings. Its date is disputed, late 12th century or after 1436.

Treasure-hunt clue: the frieze over the west door is an ancient calendar of the Attic festivals with the signs of the zodiac, set in place as decoration. Tradition puts a temple of Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth, beneath it.

Built in the mid-11th century, Sotira Lykodimou is the largest medieval building in the city. Bavarian-era Athens sold it to Russia in 1847; it reopened as the Russian church in 1855 with a separate bell tower. A cistern of an ancient aqueduct lies 5 m below the floor: ask about it. Stories of tunnels and a temple of Apollo are weak.

In the courtyard of Hadrian's Library lie the foundations of a 5th-century tetraconch, a church with four apses (15.42 m square, by Travlos), later replaced by the Megali Panagia basilica. Clue: trace the four apses on the ground.

Above the Theatre of Dionysus, a cave in the rock face holds the chapel of Our Lady of the Golden Cave, inside the front of the choregic monument of Thrasyllos. Two columns that once held victory tripods still stand above.

The 11th-century church that sits in the middle of the shopping street was due to be demolished in the new town plan; Ludwig I of Bavaria, the king's father, intervened. Clue: inscriptions and Roman capitals on the west wall.

A UNESCO-listed 11th-century monastery on the Sacred Way to Eleusis, with gold mosaics, among them the severe Pantokrator in the dome. Cistercian monks held it under the Franks. An anchor of the Byzantine era.

In a wooded valley of Hymettus above the city, an 11th-century monastery with its bath house and refectory. Its spring, the Kallopoula, flows from a carved ram's head and was said to cure infertility.

On Mitropoleos a vaulted single-aisle church stands under the stilts of a big postwar block: Patroklos Karantinos's Ministry of Education, built over it in the 1950s. The historian Biris wrote that the chapel had been 'disfigured and humiliated' under 'an ugly building'. The ministry left in 2007 and the block has stood empty since.

Agia Dynami is linked to the War of Independence: monks are said to have made cartridges here, and a stair is said to lead to a deep room (the same story is told of the Russian Church). A tunnel to the Ilisos is legend. It keeps relics of St Nikolaos Planas, Papadiamantis's confessor.
Clue: stand inside the porch and look up; the building is the sky.

Halfway up Lycabettus, the church of Agioi Isidoroi has its sanctuary in the hill's largest cave; the living rock is behind the altar and a small spring runs from it. The church burned in 1930 and was rebuilt in 1931.

A plaque speaks of a tunnel from here to Galatsi or Penteli: legend. Next to it are the cave of St Aristides and, deeper in the rock, the 1936 shelter. Expect police tape at times; a body was found in the cave in 2026.

Leo von Klenze, Ludwig I's architect, designed this cathedral, revised by Kaftanzoglou; it was built 1853–65 and completed in 1891. Its green Tinos-marble columns were cut for the royal palace, became spare when the palace was redesigned, and came here on a French warship.
Clue for a chemist: count the columns (12 in the nave, 16 in all) and look at the green serpentinite breccia against the Pentelic floor.
The British community's church (1843), neo-Gothic in bluish-grey Hymettus marble, the stone the ancients used before they turned to white Pentelic. It has the oldest church organ in Athens.
Lysandros Kaftanzoglou's large church, begun in 1871 and finished in 1905, a monument of Greek neo-Byzantine revival in a now rough part of town.
A huge domed church on Acharnon Street, called the largest in Athens; the new church was founded in 1910 on the site of a chapel linked to a grieving mother's vow.

Karl Bensel's church for the German Evangelical community (1931–34) is the most modern religious building of interwar Athens: a plain, clear volume in the Neue Sachlichkeit manner. Inside, the pulpit, pews, candlesticks and organ gallery are original.
It is linked to the Philadelphia club, the first Goethe Institute. Go on a Sunday morning.
Across from Beth Shalom, the older synagogue of Athens's Romaniote Jews, who spoke Greek and had lived in Greece since antiquity. Visits by arrangement with the Community.
The large cathedral (1842–62) built with stone from demolished churches; it dwarfs the Little Metropolis beside it. A treasury museum opened recently. Anchor of the 19th-century era.

loumbardiaris.t: Agios Dimitrios Loumbardiaris and the Pikionis paths
p: Between the Acropolis and Philopappou, Dimitris Pikionis laid out paths, steps and resting places in 1954–58 from the debris of demolished neoclassical houses: marble door frames, roof tiles, cobbles and concrete set in patterns. At the centre stands the post-Byzantine chapel of Agios Dimitrios Loumbardiaris, which he re-clad, and a small pavilion meant as a simple café.

The name 'Loumbardiaris' comes from the Ottoman cannon (lumbarda) on the hill; legend says a lightning strike on 26 October 1656 destroyed it as it was about to fire on the faithful. Frescoes of 1735 were found inside.
The works were declared a monument in 1996. Clue: find neoclassical marble fragments reused in the paving and the walls. Pikionis turned away from his own modernist school (Pefkakia) to make this.

Sthenis Molfesis and Thymios Papagiannis designed this church in 1961, published as one of the rare modern Orthodox church designs. Whether it was built to that design is unknown: go and compare with the published plan.

Built 1956–62 to designs by Paraskevi Tsatiri with I. Theodorou, one of very few women church architects of the period. The old church was moved to make way for Vouliagmenis Avenue and kept as a chapel.

Athens was the only EU capital without an official mosque until this one opened on 2 November 2020, after decades of argument. The state built it in a former naval yard: a plain box with no minaret, for 350 men and 50 women, called an 'anti-monument'.
Most of the city's Muslims still pray in about 100 unofficial rooms in basements and garages (2017 estimate). Clue: the mihrab niche pointing to Mecca.

Opened in 1837, the First Cemetery holds the city's great and good in marble: Yannoulis Halepas's 'Sleeping Maiden', Schliemann's tomb shaped like a temple with a frieze of his excavations, prime ministers, poets and Katsimbalis, Henry Miller's 'Colossus of Maroussi'.
It climbs a hill behind the Olympic stadium; quiet, shaded, full of cats. Plan an hour.

Louis de Soissons laid out this cemetery on a gentle slope with the headstones facing the sea and no high walls. About 2,050 war dead lie here (counts vary even within the CWGC), and the Athens Memorial names some 2,870 more with no known grave.
Clue: find the different faith symbols on the stones: Gurkha and Baluchi Muslim plots, and a Crimean War plot. A designed landscape cemetery of the kind Kon likes.

Inaugurated on 28 September 1975, the cemetery at Rapendosa near Dionysos holds 9,905 German dead of the Second World War and 68 of the First, about 850 in each of 12 crypts under three walled courtyards; 843 missing are named on tablets. Among them are reportedly seven women and Moroccan soldiers.
The pines burned in 1998 and were replanted. Clue: the crypt covers in the courtyard floors. A stone path from here leads to the chapels of Agios Nikitas and Agios Loukas (lead).

Opened in 1934–36 and extended in 1942, the Third Cemetery has over 27,000 monuments and about 35,000 burials. It has a Jewish section since 1946 (vandalised), Italian Occupation, Catholic and military plots, and memorials to the Kokkinia Blockade, the Aigaleo massacre, Jewish soldiers and the Holocaust.
Clue: find the two Jewish memorials. The Blockade dead lie here; combine with the Mantra.

You know it; the point here is the details. The Parthenon has almost no straight lines: the stylobate (top step) rises about 6 cm in the middle of the short sides and 11 cm on the long sides, the columns swell slightly (entasis) and lean inwards, and the corner columns are thicker. Crouch at a corner and sight along the north or south step in low light: you can see the curve.

On 26 September 1687 a Venetian mortar fired by Morosini's army from Philopappou hit the gunpowder the Ottomans had stored in the Parthenon. About 300 people died and the middle of the temple blew out; Morosini then broke the west pediment's Poseidon group trying to take it home. The Propylaia had already been wrecked by a powder explosion in 1656, and the Ottomans dismantled the Nike temple for a gun battery.

The restorers' story is visible too. Nikolaos Balanos's iron clamps of the early 1900s rusted and split the marble; since 1975 the Acropolis Restoration Service has replaced them with titanium and filled gaps with new Pentelic marble, the bright white blocks you can spot among the honey-coloured old ones. A Mycenaean wall section is being opened to visitors.
acropolis.s: Stevens (Hesperia 1943); hh.gr; cnn.gr; Protothema (Apr 2025); History Today.

p: Closed for years, the North Slope reopened on 1 June 2025 with Onassis funding, and it is the quietest part of the Acropolis ticket. The Peripatos path circles the rock past caves: Apollo Hypoakraios with niches for votive plaques of the archons, Zeus, and Pan, whose cult came to Athens after Marathon.

Find-it details: an inscription at the foot of an upright limestone block gives the length of the Peripatos as 5 stades 18 feet; the Klepsydra spring, used since the Neolithic, seeps where porous limestone sits on impermeable schist (geology you can see); the Aglaureion, the largest cave (14 × 22 m), identified in 1980 from an inscription of 247/6 BC.
Ruins of the post-Byzantine chapel of Agios Nikolaos lie near the Pan shrine.

The theatre where Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes were first staged, rebuilt in stone in the 4th century BC and refitted by the Romans. Its front row has 67 marble thrones carved with the titles of officials; the centre one belonged to the priest of Dionysus Eleuthereus (IG II² 5022).

Find-it: on the priest's throne, lion paws, satyrs and, under the inscription, two kneeling Persians holding griffins. The marble orchestra paving and the barrier round it are Nero-era, built when the theatre hosted beast shows. The open-air lapidarium has a victor's base with faint wreaths.

Below the Acropolis lay the civic centre: council house, law courts, the Tholos where the presidents dined, shops and the stoas where Socrates argued. The Hephaisteion on the hill, called the 'Theseion' since the Middle Ages, is the best-preserved temple in Greece; the Stoa of Attalos was rebuilt in 1953–56 on its original foundations and holds the museum.

Find-it: by the Tholos at the south-west corner, a marble post of about 500 BC reads, right to left, 'HOROS EIMI TES AGORAS' — 'I am the boundary of the Agora' (IG I³ 1087). A second one is under the Middle Stoa. At the Stoa of Attalos, look at its north end for original ancient blocks among the 1950s rebuild.
Upgrades (new paths, rest spots) were finished in 2026 along with Kerameikos.

roman-agora.t: Roman Agora and Tower of the Winds
p: The Tower of the Winds, built by Andronikos of Kyrrhos (2nd–mid 1st century BC), is a 12.8 m octagon of Pentelic marble. Each face carries a relief of the wind blowing from that direction, with its name. A bronze Triton weathervane once turned on top (Vitruvius describes it).

It was a scientific instrument. Under each relief are the lines of a sundial: in raking light you can read them. Inside (open since 2014–16), channels in the floor belonged to a water clock fed from an Acropolis spring, with a reservoir annex on the south side. It later served as a church and, in the 18th century, as a dervish lodge.
Next to it: the Roman latrines, the Medrese gate and the Fethiye mosque.

Kerameikos, the potters' quarter, was the city's main gate and cemetery. The Sacred Way left for Eleusis through the Sacred Gate, and the Panathenaic procession started at the Dipylon; Pericles gave his funeral speech here. The Street of Tombs keeps Classical family plots with stelai (the famous ones like Hegeso are casts; the originals are in the National Museum).

Find-it: the Eridanos stream still runs through the Sacred Gate in its stone channel, under a small arched bridge (dry in summer). On the Pompeion ramp, wheel ruts. In the lower courses of the Themistoclean Wall (479/8 BC), reused grave stelai and bases, evidence of how fast the wall was built after the Persians left.
The site reopened on 15 September 2026 after a 2023–26 upgrade with new paths and views.

Begun by the Peisistratids in the 6th century BC and finished by Hadrian in AD 132, the temple had 104 columns; 15 stand. One blew down in a storm in 1852 and lies where it fell, its drums like a sliced loaf: look at the 24 flutes and the dowel sockets.

Hadrian's Arch is free to see. Its two inscriptions face opposite ways: 'This is Athens, the old city of Theseus' and 'This is the city of Hadrian, not of Theseus'. A hermit once lived on the temple's architrave; the date of the 'stylite hut' is disputed.

On this hill the citizens of Athens met in assembly; Themistocles, Pericles and Demosthenes spoke from the rock-cut bema, about 8.35 m wide with side steps (its last phase c. 340–330 BC). The view to the Acropolis is the one they had.

Find-it: east of the bema, 58 small niches cut in the rock held votive plaques to Zeus Hypsistos, a healing god of later antiquity (Forsén 1993). Look also for the cuttings of two unfinished stoas and for the quarry marks. The astronomer Meton set up a heliotropion here in 433 BC; no trace is known.

Inventories of the 330s BC count 372 shipsheds in the harbours of Piraeus, 196 of them at Zea (today's Pasalimani). Their remains run under the modern town. At Akti Moutsopoulou and Sirangiou you can see slipways, the keel groove and column bases through the street windows of a basement, dug by Dragatsis in the 1880s.
The Zea Harbour Project found double sheds about 80 m long. This is where the fleet of Salamis was kept dry.

Rebuilt in marble for the first modern Olympics (1896) on the Roman stadium of Herodes Atticus. The vaulted tunnel under the east bank, about 57 m long, is said to be the only intact ancient part; it now leads to the Olympic torch museum. Double-faced herms at the curved end (originals or casts? check). Herodes's tomb lay on Ardettos hill above.

The hill of Ares below the Acropolis was the seat of the oldest court; tradition says St Paul preached here (Acts 17), recorded on a bronze plaque at the foot. The polished rock steps are slippery; a 2025 project reworked the plateau.

Below Parliament, a relief of a dying hoplite modelled on a figure from the Aegina temple pediment, with lines from Pericles's funeral speech and the names of battles (the list keeps growing). The Evzones change guard every hour.

In Monastiraki station (Line 3) a 24 m glass walkway crosses a 300 m² excavation where the Eridanos, Athens's buried river, still flows in its vaulted channel of Hadrian's time: 40–50 m³ an hour, about 80 after storms. Stand still and listen.
Old Line 1 signs at street level still read 'MONASTIRION' from 1895.

The metro dig at Syntagma (about 500 m²) found 35 graves, a bronze foundry, a stretch of the Eridanos bed and the Peisistratid aqueduct. A wall of the concourse shows the stratigraphy from antiquity to the 19th century, and a woman's skeleton of the 4th century BC lies in a case.

acharnian-gate.t: Acharnian Gate in the National Bank
p: When the National Bank built its new wing on Aiolou, it found the Acharnian Gate of the Themistoclean Wall and kept it: about 30 m of wall, the road through the gate with cart ruts and the moat, 5.1 m below the street, visible from the building.
A planned underground car park under Kotzia Square uncovered three ancient streets, a cemetery and workshops; the car park was abandoned and the dig left open behind railings.
At Elaionas station, the piers of an ancient bridge over the Kifisos plain are displayed: called the oldest bridge found in Greece.
The Long Walls of the 5th century BC made Athens and Piraeus one fortress. Traces survive along Thessalonikis Street, under building pilotis near Tavros station and as a tower in Moschato.

Found only in 1996 while digging for a museum, the remains of the Lyceum's palaestra mark where Aristotle taught from 335 BC, walking with his students. Modest ruins; a big name. Upgrades and digital tours were announced in 2026.

The grove of Akademos, where Plato founded his school, is a scruffy park with the remains of a gymnasium, a square peristyle and the 'Sacred House'. Few visitors; one of the most important names in philosophy.
Hadrian built a library-and-garden complex here in AD 132; its western colonnade faces Monastiraki Square. In the courtyard lie the foundations of the four-apsed early church (see Megali Panagia).

The marble temple of Poseidon (444–440 BC) stands high above the sea at the tip of Attica. It is built of local Agrileza marble from Lavreotiki, not Pentelic; four of its drums are at Chatsworth in England.

Find-it: 'BYRON' is carved on a column; that he did it himself is legend, and its position is disputed (first column on the right, lowest drum, or a south column). Visitors may not enter the temple, so bring a zoom. Dozens of 18th–19th-century travellers' names are cut beside it.

The Soros covers the 192 Athenians killed at Marathon. Schliemann dug in 1884 and found nothing; Stais found the cremation layer in 1890–91. The museum has the Ionic capital of the victory trophy and Egyptian-style statues from Herodes Atticus's sanctuary at Brexiza. The Plataean tumulus nearby was excavated in 1970.

At Brauron Athenian girls served Artemis as arktoi, 'bears'. The site keeps a stone bridge of the 420s BC with wheel grooves, the sacred spring, cave shrines and a Π-shaped stoa. Silting has moved the sea about 400 m away. The 'tomb of Iphigenia' is legend.
For two thousand years initiates walked the Sacred Way from Kerameikos to Eleusis for the Mysteries of Demeter. Today the sanctuary sits among refineries and cement works, which is part of its power.

Find-it: by the Greater Propylaea, a giant bust (probably Marcus Aurelius) from the pediment has a Christian cross scratched into the Gorgon on its breastplate. The Kallichoron well, where Demeter sat mourning, made the builders cut the lowest Propylaea step short. The Ploutonion cave, the door to the underworld, is behind.
An abandoned junction of the dead Peloponnese metre-gauge network with rusting trains on its sidings, about 2 hours from Athens.
Unverified since 2018; check recent photos before going.
The family house of the inventor of the Pap test, now a museum, about 2 hours from Athens.
Short hours (e.g. Tue and Thu evenings, Sat morning); check before going.
An 'almost anti-plastic' modern chapel built in 1960 by the architect Giannakis on the summit of Kithairon during his military service, near the old NIKE flight.
Lead, not verified; mountain access.
Greece's first crematorium (30 Sept 2019), by MONOGON architects, about 80 km from Athens; the end of a long religious and legal fight.
Working crematorium; exterior.

routes.name: Acropolis, the hills and the Observatory
routes.when: Start at the Acropolis opening slot; the Observatory visitor centre opens in the evening, so end there or come back.
routes.summary: The Acropolis for its curves and scars, the quiet North Slope caves, the Theatre of Dionysus, then over the Areopagus to Pikionis's paths, the Pnyx and the Observatory hill.

routes.name: Agora, Monastiraki and Psyrri
routes.summary: From the boundary stone of the Agora through Hadrian's Library and the Eridanos in the metro to the Tower of the Winds, the Medrese gate, the churches built of other buildings, the column chapel and the Kerameikos gate.

routes.name: Syntagma and Panepistimiou: Occupation and ideas
routes.when: Do Korai 4 in the morning (Tue–Sat 9–14); Old Chemistry library Mon–Fri.
routes.summary: The Unknown Soldier and the metro strata, the Gestapo house and the Kommandantur cells, Zonar's, Parnassos and Koun's basement theatre, the old National Library and the Catholic cathedral, ending at the Old Chemistry lab.

routes.name: Market and Omonia
routes.when: Lunchtime for Diporto; the bank opens on weekdays.
routes.summary: Down Athinas and Aiolou: the Themistoclean gate inside a bank, the car park that became a dig, a sign-less basement tavern, Kaftanzoglou's Omonia church and the vanished railway square.

routes.name: Plaka, the Olympieion and the buried river
routes.when: Cemetery 7:30–20; Saita and Brettos in the evening.
routes.summary: From Zenetos's sliding façade by the Garden through the Russian and Anglican churches to Hadrian's temple and arch, the open Ilisos, the stadium tunnel, the Ardittos shelter hill and the First Cemetery.

routes.name: Kolonaki and Lycabettus
routes.when: Climb to Agioi Isidoroi before noon; the theatre only on concert nights.
routes.summary: Modernist blocks round the National Garden's edge, the Conservatory and the Lyceum, the column of Kolonaki and Papadiamantis's square, Pikionis's school and the German church, then up to the cave church, its shelter and Zenetos's theatre.

routes.name: Exarchia, Alexandras and Kypseli
routes.summary: The Polytechnic gate, the Blue Building and the Exarchia cinemas, Atelier 66's street stair, the junta's Bouboulinas site, the Averof stele and the Prosfygika, then Kypseli's 1930s street and a shelter with its steel doors.

routes.name: Ambelokipi and Goudi: towers, the junta and science
routes.when: Criminology Museum by appointment only; Mineralogy Museum Mon–Fri 9:30–14.
routes.summary: The glass towers of the 1970s, the junta's last Security HQ, Valsamakis's first block, the Pasteur Institute, the last guillotine, the Olympic badminton hall and the brutalist student slab of Zografou.

routes.name: West Athens: Finos to Votanikos
routes.summary: Finos Film's building, the Peloponnese station, Plato's Academy, the only Ottoman fountain, the city's first mosque and the train turned theatre.

routes.name: Piraeus: ships, shelters and the Blockade
routes.when: Mantra mornings Tue–Fri; Lipasmata park open late.
routes.summary: Trireme sheds through a basement window, the Kastella shelters and the 1960s cave club, the old kafeneia and German batteries, the ghost factories, the fertiliser park and the dragon power station, then Nikaia's Blockade wall and cemetery.

routes.name: The south shore: power, Olympics and refugees
routes.when: EMST closed Monday; Phaleron cemetery daytime.
routes.summary: FIX's façades and Dourgouti's refugee blocks, Nea Smyrni's December 1944, the 1903 power station and the beach-volleyball white elephant, the sea-facing war cemetery, Zenetos's round school and the Panagoulis station, down to the old airport and Glyfada's modern churches.

routes.name: Kaisariani and Hymettus
routes.summary: The wall of the 200, the refugee blocks of 'Little Moscow', the monastery spring and the German station ruins near the summit.

routes.name: Penteli and the north (car)
routes.when: Car needed. End at the Newall telescope for an evening show.
routes.summary: Workers' housing and a cave in the suburbs, the one-day church of Galatsi, the junta broadcasting house and the reactor, the sanatorium shells, the NATO dishes, the Parthenon's quarry cave, the German cemetery and the marble telescope.

routes.name: Mesogeia, Lavrio and Sounion (car)
routes.when: Car needed; a full day. Sounion at sunset.
routes.summary: Brauron's bridge and pillboxes at Porto Rafti, the NIKE missile base, Lavrio's ore washeries and railway, then Sounion for Byron's name.

tours.name: Church hunt through the ages: one day in the centre
tours.intro: Athens's religious buildings are best where one era sits inside another: a column through a roof, a church made of carvings, a chapel under a ministry, a cave church, a Bauhaus pulpit, a mosque with no minaret. One clue per stop.
tours.how: On foot plus one metro hop to Votanikos (or end at Loumbardiaris). Churches open mornings; the Christuskirche only on Sunday, Agioi Isidoroi 9–12.
story: Athens was a small town when it became the capital in 1834, and the planners of King Otto demolished dozens of Byzantine churches to lay out the new streets; the survivors are scattered among shops and offices. That is why the hunt is good here: every old church is a survivor of a plan.
The order is chronological: early Christian foundations, Byzantine churches built of spolia, Ottoman-era chapels, the Bavarian 19th century, then the modernists and the new mosque.

stops.note: 5th century: trace four apses in the courtyard of Hadrian's Library.
Roman column through a chapel roof; fevers were tied to it with thread. Find the capital among the branches.
12th century (disputed): a church made of about 90 older carvings. Find the calendar frieze of months and zodiac.
11th century, saved by Ludwig I. Find the Roman capitals in the west wall.
11th century, Russian since 1847. Ask about the cistern 5 m under the floor.
Ottoman-era chapel under a 1950s ministry on stilts. Look up: the building is its sky.
1853–65, Klenze. Count the green Tinos columns cut for a palace.
1931–34, Neue Sachlichkeit: Bauhaus-era pulpit and candlesticks (Sunday).
15th–16th century in Lycabettus's biggest cave; read the tunnel plaque.
1954–58, Pikionis: a chapel re-clad in the debris of demolished Athens. Find the neoclassical marble scraps.
2020: the state-built mosque without a minaret. Find the mihrab.

tours.name: Occupied Athens, 1941–44
tours.intro: The Occupation left exact marks: cells with prisoners' graffiti, an execution wall, a factory yard with ricochet scars, a synagogue where a community was rounded up.
tours.how: Two half-days: the centre on foot (Korai 4 Tue–Sat 9–14), then Kaisariani by bus and Nikaia by metro (Mantra Tue–Fri 9–13).
story: Germany, Italy and Bulgaria occupied Greece from April 1941. In Athens the famine of the first winter killed tens of thousands; the resistance (EAM-ELAS) grew strong in the refugee suburbs, and the occupiers answered with reprisals and with 'blockades' of whole districts, where hooded informers picked out men to be shot.

In 1943–44 Haidari camp fed the execution grounds. The Jews of Athens were arrested at their synagogue on 24 March 1944. The Germans left on 12 October 1944; the Dekemvriana fighting between ELAS and the British-backed government followed within weeks.

stops.note: Seat of the German military administration.
SS and Gestapo interrogation centre; the cell door survives.
Kommandantur cells: prisoners' graffiti 6 m underground.
Two waiters arrived in Nazi uniform in 1941, fifth-column spies.
24 March 1944: the round-up of the Jews of Athens.
1 May 1944: 200 shot; they went singing.
The condemned block of the camp.
17 August 1944: the Blockade's execution yard.
Where the Blockade dead lie.
October 1944: ELAS saves the power station from demolition.

tours.name: The junta: torture rooms, a bomb and a gate
tours.intro: The colonels ruled from 21 April 1967 to July 1974. Their places of torture and the places of resistance are small, scattered and mostly unmarked.
tours.how: Centre on foot, then metro to Ambelokipi; Loumbarda and the Panagoulis station by car or tram.
story: On 21 April 1967 a group of colonels took power with tanks from Goudi. Opponents were jailed, tortured and exiled to islands. The Security Police ran Bouboulinas 18 and then Mesogeion 14–18; the Military Police ran EAT-ESA.

Alexandros Panagoulis tried to kill the dictator Papadopoulos in August 1968; the Polytechnic rose in November 1973; the regime fell in July 1974 after the Cyprus disaster. Panagoulis died in a car crash in 1976 that many still think was not an accident.

stops.note: Security HQ to 1971: the rooftop falanga room. Demolished.
Averof prison, demolished 1972.
17 November 1973: the gate a tank crushed.
Where the November 1973 mobilisations began.
The Military Police torture rooms, where Panagoulis was held.
Security HQ 1971–74: two cells survive.
The junta's broadcasting house (begun 1968).
A tower allowed by the junta's relaxed height law.
13 August 1968: Panagoulis's bomb under the coast road.
1 May 1976: where he died.

tours.name: The water of Athens: buried rivers and a marble dam
tours.intro: Athens has always been short of water. Follow it from the tyrants' aqueduct and the buried Eridanos and Ilisos to an Ottoman fountain and the marble-faced dam of 1929.
tours.how: Centre on foot and metro; Marathon dam by car.
story: The ancient city drank from springs and wells, aqueducts built by the Peisistratids and by Hadrian, and the rivers Eridanos and Ilisos. Both rivers now run under the streets: the Eridanos in a Roman channel, the Ilisos under an avenue since the 1930s.
Hadrian's aqueduct served Athens into the 20th century. Only the American Ulen company's Marathon dam (1929) and its tunnel ended the shortages.

stops.note: 6th century BC: the tyrants' aqueduct in Evangelismos station.
The Eridanos bed and the aqueduct in the stratigraphy wall.
The Eridanos still flowing; listen.
The Eridanos leaves the city through the Sacred Gate.
64 seats over running water.
The Tower of the Winds' water clock.
The Klepsydra spring, where limestone meets schist.
Hadrian's reservoir, still in use under the café.

tours.name: Science in Athens: telescopes, labs and a reactor
tours.intro: For a chemist: Ziller's laboratory with its hidden radio, an observatory Gagarin visited, a marble-housed telescope, the Pasteur Institute, minerals and a reactor.
tours.how: Old Chemistry on a weekday; observatories in the evening (book); Penteli and Agia Paraskevi by car.
story: Science came to Athens with the Bavarian state: the Observatory (1842) and the university laboratories. Chemistry got its own building in 1887–90, in the age of Hofmann and Christomanos; physics, medicine and bacteriology followed.
After the war the Demokritos centre and its reactor (1961) were Greece's step into nuclear research.

tours.name: Mountains of Attica: sanatoria and Cold War ruins
tours.intro: The hills round Athens hold two layers of ruins: the 1930s sanatoria of the 'Greek Davos' and the radar, radio and missile sites of the Cold War.
tours.how: Car needed; two days (Penteli and Parnitha; Keratea with Lavrio). Stay outside fences.
story: Penteli's and Parnitha's dry air drew tuberculosis sanatoria between the wars. After antibiotics they became hospitals, hotels and schools, and then ruins.

In the Cold War the same hills carried NATO: NIKE missile flights at Keratea, Hymettus, Parnitha and Kithairon from 1960, with US custody of the nuclear warheads; telecom stations on Penteli; a US Navy station at Nea Makri. Most closed by 1990–2005.

tours.name: Modern Athens: Pikionis, Zenetos, Konstantinidis
tours.intro: The best Greek modernists in their own city: Pikionis's turn from modernism to landscape, Zenetos's machines, Konstantinidis's frames, and the interwar blocks that came first.
tours.how: Centre on foot; Nea Filadelfeia and Agios Dimitrios by metro.
story: Athens built one of Europe's best sets of 1930s modernist apartment blocks, in Kypseli, Exarchia and Kolonaki. After the war the polykatoikia became the city's mass housing; a few architects used it to experiment.

Pikionis abandoned his modernist school for the Philopappou paths; Zenetos designed for a future of electronic cities; Konstantinidis built bare frames with earth-coloured infill. Several of their works are already gone.

story: Classical Athens is mostly ruins in a modern city, so the pleasure is in the details: a stone that speaks, a curve in a step, a river still running.
